div.head: M 0 DO U LL's k- PATENT SELF-It AISIN FLU BBST MAKES TUB PASIRT
div.p: M 0 DO U LL's k- PATENT SELF-It AISIN FLU BBST MAKES TUB PASIRT
-IJSTRATED FASHIONS,

There is a tendency in the world of dress to give visible expression to our inward sentiments of loyalty by affecting a combination of red, white and blue—the Coronation colours. It is not, however, a very easy matter always to at- tain to success, as much experience and no small amount of good taste must be employed if any- thing but an nnpleasing effect is to be produced. Red also should only be employed as a pleasing note of contrast, and introduced with discrimin- ation. One hears horrible rumours that even the masculine dress is to follow suit in regard to colouring, and the bare idea calls up grotesque visions of gaily-garbed oddities. Imagine being called on to "honour and obey" a .inan wearing a bright navy blue snit, scarlet tie and waist- coat, with a white hat, gloves and shoes, as the June brides might have to do! Red is too hot looking and bright a colour to my fancy for the brilliant days of summer, unless introduced in the form of a sunshade, or limited to the narrow strappings or pipings which embellish many tailor-made gowns at present. Should the Coronation Day prove it- self worthy of the occasion, and be brilliant and warm, there are several ideas which suggest themselves to my mind as the most successful methods of combining a desire to be loyal with good taste, and a toilette at once becoming and fashionable. The illustration depicts a dress of navy blue voile of a good shade made over white

div.head: MD, WHITE AND BLU:
div.p: MD, WHITE AND BLU:

thongh a less easily soiled lining could be emplqwed if ,desired. It is trimmed with white satin strapping s piped at either edge with red, the chemisette and undersleeves being of white lace. It is completed by a white straw hat trimmed with poppies, and a red sunshade, all the reds being of one and the same tore. A white silk and lace petticoat and white shoes and gloves should be the finishing touches of this chic dreas.

Another more dressy toilette could be of thin white spotted muslin sprigged with blue flowers and made with numerous small flounces bordered -with narrow blue ribbon run on just above an edging of lace. A red waistband, and a touch of red at the neck could be effectively introduced, while a floral toque of cornflowers and poppies would further the scheme of colour. The sun- shade should in this instance be of white silk sprigged with blue flowers and bordered with red. A red silk petticoat would emphasize this note of colour if desired.

There are many little odds and ends of the toilette, such as buckles, brooches and buttons, which, in the form of the royal monogram, crown, or crest are extremely tasteful and pretty, and should be Used either in enamel, gold or jewels for the two dresses just described. For evening wear I recently saw some fascinat- ing golden slippers with a jewelled buckle in the form of a crown, which made .one's mind

div.head: 'PRETTY BLOUSE.
div.p: A 'PRETTY BLOUSE.

turn to Cinderella and her dainty foot-gear. Fashion and her exponents are exercising all the ingenuity possible to produce novelties which are expressive of the National event of this season. The pretty evening blouse illus- trated is of white d'eyrit net and eau lace, a large clam of pink ribbons arranged to simulate .a large rose, and tiny ones to match appearing at the point where the elbow sleeves cease and the fall of lace commences over the, lower part of the arm. A compiete gown carried out on the same lines would look extremely pretty, especially if made over very pale pink silk of a tint resembling the outer petals of a rose.

This charming tea-gown was made by a well, known firm for a lady renowned for her good taste in clothes. It is of the softest, richest Oriental satin of a delicate tone of rieux rose. It fits the figure easily but closely, and has a low trained skirt beautified by some dainty open-work worked in silks to match the satin, and tiny tucks at the hem. The neck, which opens in a V shape, has a fall of creamy lace which extends fichu.wise down the front, being caught at intervals with bows of satin ribbon The edge of the lace next the throat is softened by a few folding chiffon, while the sleeves come just to the elbow, and are finished by a fall of law.canght at the elbow by a satin bow. There

div.head: CHARM NO TEA-GOWN..
div.p: CHARM NO TEA-GOWN..

is nothing very elaborate in the gown, which could be copied in almost any material; it is only in the arrangement of the lace that con- siderable care is required. Sleeves are this season showing a wonderful amount of originality in their fashioning, and most of those most affected show a wide puff just above the wrist, the rest and upper part of the sleeve being nearly tight-fitting, and in many instances profusely tucked and lace adorned. This bagging style of sleeve is much in vogue whether for day or evening wear, and in very thin materials the baggy fulness often starts from much higher up the arm, which is only confined by a band of lace for a few inches below the shoulder,
COQUETTI.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

[ALL RIGHTS REssuvE.D.] There seems considerable deribt whether the King belongs to the House of Saxe Coburg, or the o Ml I NTJBER 6Pk House _RADEI Hanover. In Whitaker's Almanac, and also in the Almanac de Gotha, King Edward VII. is given as the firet Sovereign in the House of Saxe Coburg. The same oescription can be found in several other official publics- tious, yet this is contrary to precedent, as in our history it has been customary for the son of a reigning Queen to belong to the dynasty of big mother. Consequently, unless a change is to be made, King Edward belongs to the House of Hanover, and Mr Stead, in his" Kings and Queens of England," takes this view. It seems strange that the matter should have been left to become the sub- ject- of dispute, and no doubt an authoritative statement will shortly be made about it. • Many private mansions in London have been placed at the disposal of the King for the use of His Majesty's guests for the Coronation. Amongst others may be mentioned Dorchester House, Chesterfield House, and Wimborne House. Many well known hostesses will also make a point of extending hospitality to the Colonial visitors. There is a general feeling that the Colonials have rendered invaluable services during the war ; and it is consequently only natural that there should be a corresponding desire to render every honour to the distinguished colonial visitors who are coming ever for the Coronation. Princess Louise, who remembers much of Canada will give a garden party at Kensington Pace, and her Rosa I Highness was most hospitable to the Colonial visitors at the time of the Jubilee. The King has offered Pembroke Lodge, one of the numerous royal residences in the neighbourhood of Richmond,to Princess Louise (Duchess of Argyll). Until Prineess Louise inherited Kent Cottage in the Isle of Wight, uncer the late Queen's will, Her Royal Highness had no residence of her own in England, but she is now the near neighbour of Princess Henry of Battenberg both in London, and the Isle of Wight. Each has a suite lof nartments at Kensington Palace, where Princess &Tony possesses a London residence of her own for the I first time.

Some of the Free Churches are refusing on principle to lend remise for Coronation feasts unless it is stipulated that alcoholic drinks shalt not be served, and ono writer says be understands that, in lieu of alcoholic drink. lemonade, tea, and coffee, will be provided. That may be a very good idea, but it is to be hoped that tea and coffee really will be provided. At the majority of popular gathericge, where tea, coffee, also cocoa are announced, it is impossible to tell which is which, and all the consumer can do is to try all three, and select the least nasty decoction. The craze for hot water drinking continues, this " beverage" being served at fashionable luncheon and dinner tables, in little silver tankards. Many things are urged for and against this practice of hot water drink- ing, but it is not pretended that it tends to decrease the use of stimulant among our sex. And if hot weer proves as debilitating inside as it does when used for utward application one can scarcely marvel at such a state of affairs. A really hot bath taken at any time, rave the last thing at night, renders one flabby to a de- grec. It would therefore appear to be wiser to abstain from becoming a hot-water drinker. Women are now wearing the wash leather gloves which have lataly become 60 conspicuous upen the smartly dressed man. They can scarcely be said to be in good I taste, and the more sensible emong us will avoid them. i One may possess the most mune taste in colours, but it is difficult to" dress up " to bright canary gloves,and the majority of women will no doubt remain content I with the more subdued shades of the suede variety. borne feminine critics declare that men have mart - regard for fine clothes than women, and if exception a prove tbe rule, they can generally point to so maey as to convince the most sceptical. However that may be' the fashion for yellow gloves shows that it is not only women who adopt any novelty marine's of the impor- tant question whether or not it suits theme, and to see a man in the conventional afternoon attire with canary coloured gloves at once strikes a jarring note. But as a matter of fact, the" gilded youth " is just as food of his fashions ae is the flightiest woman, and when he adopts mustard coloured gloves, the male fraternity is quick to follow bie example. Cashmemeepecially in white is approved by fashionable modifies, an item which will •rejoice the hearts of many of us. Of the draping qualities of csshmere, nothing remains to be said, it cleans too excellently, sad it is almost an impossibilify to wear this fabric out. Touches of green on white gowns are being much employed for young girls, and this combination is both restful and altogether suitable, Flounces.when they appear—ld:deb is frequently—have now scarcelyA any fulness in them but they are usually somewhat lavishly ornamented, and put op with piping. Piping is much in evidence, adding yet another C. the list of uld world trimmings, that have Appeared of late. .. The prediction that velvet would be much worn this year, has been fully- justified. At all the smartest weddings, receptions, dinners the wive; gown appears. and no bride of to-day considers her trousseau complete without snob an addition. It is costly, of course, but then it has a long life, if properly taken care of. And one can do almost anything with a realest gown. Should it be worn much round the hem, it may be cut away and scalloped and bung over tiny chiffon flounce,. Have the seams worn whit.? Cover them with narrow bawls of jet galon. Have the sleeves an elderly air ? Banish them, and in the place of velvet use chiffon. Then there is the visit to the dyers, which is freqiienly of the greatest tute in helping one to defy all recognition. Panne has been tried, as we all know,ae a substitutte,but it has neither the dignity or importance of velvet. It is apt to be meek when it should be self assertive. When a man unwarily sets his foot upon it, it subsides Into such flatness that he thinks it is only the carpet. Silk velvet under such circumstances doss not allow him to remain long under such a delusion. In many of the larger houses, whittle are now being done up, the internal decorations are placed in the hands of a " lady art decorator." Some are exceedingly clever in judging the methods of decoration, best suited to the style and proportions of the rooms, and their artistic services are much sought after. They mostly employ men to do the actual work, but there is little doubt that, in course of time, many women aid find employment in house decorators' work. Some are already engage& in fixing silk panels or medallions, the painting of felt zee or dodos, or in the execution of other. work in which the delimit° lingers of women are • dis- tinct advantage. Annie Swan's new novel " Love Grown Cold " (Methuen) is unquestionably one of the strongest she has yet given us. Tbere can be little doubt that the characters are taken from life, and Angus and Jane, Eadie are among those that beat express Annie Swan'a philosophy of life. Tbey are good and upright, aod remain firm to the cld,truths, and the old ideal,. MADGE.

div.head: CHEEKY IMPOSITION.
div.p: A CHEEKY IMPOSITION.

A local lady had what sbe described as "a cheeky Imposition " playcd upon bar the other day by an un- scrupulous store kecper. She bad asked for a box et Bile Beans and had paid for them, when she discovered that they aere,not the teal original Chas. Porde'. Bite Beans but some inferior I:separation. Our informant describes what followed : •• Do you call yourself an honest man " she asked, thumping the box on the counter. The shopman looked amazed and tried to look hurt.

" You asked fcr a box of Bile Beans, madam, and you have got it. you--' " I have done nettling of the kind ! "she went on in I a still higher key, " I call it a cheeky imposition ! You know that there is only one real genuine Bile Beane, but because I didn't happen to say Chas. Forde's Bile Beans you trot out this rubbish ! " " You will find those Beans just as good ••••" "Bear the man !" shouted the now irate purchaser " Just as good ! Chae. Forde's Bile Beans brought me from e bra of sickness and put me on my feet again,and you palm off this musty old uns=iesbli, stuff and eV it is just as good as the real Bile beans 1 Yeu'll tt 11 inc that black is really the same as white next I Give tThr Chas Forde's Bile Beans or my money back." There- upon the storekeeper, Ir oking very red and uncornfnr- able, produced a box of Chas- Fr,rde's Bile Beans. Pick- ing it up,the lady walked to the door and then remarked " Look you here Mr Bterekeeper, you've lost four go-d customers by this bit of trickery. I shall never come into year shop again, and I can promise that at least three others to whom I shall tell what has cremated will buy elsewhere from tc-day. Good afternoon !" The above incident forcibly illustrates the, need of the warnings issued by the Bile Bean Co. of 119, Lana on Will, E.C. that purchasers of Bile Beans shall see the name Chas Forth' on every box and refuse all without it, A bcx will be pent pcst tree frcm keadquarters upon receipt of prices one and three-ball-pence or two and nine.
Death and Funeral of Mr. G. C. Dewhurst.

The remains of the late Mrs George Ct arnley Dewhurst were interred in the parish churchyard at Lymm the other afternoon. Mrs Dewhurst, who died at Bath, on Wednesday week in her 71et year lived until about eight years ago at Beechwood, Lymm, and was the seccnd wife of the late Mr George C Dewburst, of Beechwood. During her Mo. time she was the leading spirit in Lymm in al matters connected with the church. The remains were net at Lymm Station and taken to Beech- wood, thence to Lymm Church, where the funeral servlce was conducted by the Rector, the Rev G B Thurston, and the Rev W G Knocker, rector cf St Peter', Oughtrington. Among the"rnournsra were Captain Robert Dewhurst (son), of Greenrnount, Clorsilla, Ireland, Colonel Wigham (trother), and es;•rs G L Dewhurst, Harry llewhurst, G Powys Dewhuret,and Arthur Dewtturst (grandsons),Walter and Charles Wigham (nephews), Mr Edward Trotter (London), and Mr it Berry (MancheQter). The bearers were Messrs G Bennett, James Cart- wright and F Parris of the Beechwood estate.

PART 11.

The next day but one was the Witham club day. 'Prom early morning the creaking of swing-boats was to be heard in the Market Place ; also the clatter of merry-go-rounds, the braying of a monster organ, the rattling of bullets in the shooting gallery, shout- ing of children, incessant chatter and laughter among buyers and sellers of ice-creams, oranges, and club cakes. Bessie's Aunt Jane had insisted on her going to her for the day, for her house commanded a good view of this market-place, and, as the good woman remarked, she was not likely to see the sight again for many a day. In the afternoon Mrs. Collins, having helped the servant to wash up the plates and dishes used at luncheon by her various lodgers, walked bare-headed to the gate of her little garden, to look at the procession which was winding its Nay along the Parade. There was the lifeboat with its brown-faced, red-capped occupants borne aloft on a waggon drawn by six horses; then came the Morris dancers—three score or more of them—stalwart youths clad in white and bedizened with ribbons and bells, who capered and gyrated with astonishing grace and agility as they passed. Three or four bands formed part. of the procession, each of which enlivened the entertainment with the tune they loved best. They passed on at length and the bystanders dispersed themselves in little knots over the green which divided the Parade from the beach. Each group had its centre of attraction : in one a troupe of "niggers " was performing, singing plantation songs which would have been pretty had not the comic member of the company so often interpolated his harsh falsetto. Another party clustered round a ventriloquist who performed wonders with two hideous wooden figures which moved their jaws in a most uncanny fashion. A little further on might be seen a conjuror, within a short distance of whom an artist of the fire-eating and sword-swallowing order electrified all beholders. Immediately in front of airs. Collins' gate a little crowd had collected round a raised wooden platform in the centre of which was a harmonium to which a large placard was appended announcing that "the Montmorency family will shortly appear." Mrs. Collins, crossingher arms on the gate, smiled to herself and hummed th 4 chorus under her breath. She was blissfully conscious of leisure and sunshine, and amusement. Like all the Witham folks she took pride and delight in the club-day celebration, though she was almost always too busy to take an active part in it. Next year perhaps, she rcilacted, she might be able to treat herself to a day's holiday, ana to devote herself comfortably and systematically to the pursuit of pleasure as exemplified in the gaictic , now in progress. There would no longer be so much need for hard work since it had become unnecessary to "lay by " for Bessie. It might be that Bessie herself would come over for the day. In spite of Jane's prophecies to the contrary Mrs. Collins was very sure that Bessie would like to come and hare an outing with her mother. They would take a carri- age, perhaps, and drive through the town. The good woman paused in her song to chuckle ecstati- cally to herself as she pictured the envy and admira- tion of her friends and neighbours. She sometimes reproached herself for not keeping more humble in her mind over the contemplation of Bessie's prospects; it was almost impossible to resist boasting of them a little when her cronies dropped in of an evening. Some of them had looked down on Mrs. Collins in the past, for it was well known that her husband had left her but poorly off, and she had only herself to look to. Nevertheless she had come out of the or- deal gallantly • she had paid her way and been be- holden to nobody, and had saved a tidy bit into the bargain. Ah ! There were the Whitesides—Mrs. White- side had been that set up because of Martha's mar- riage last year. Martha had only married a plumber and glazier when all was said and done, though he was doing a good business, and drove his own gig. What was Martha's good fortune compared with Bessie's? They were walking towards her now in the leisurely, straggling fashion peculiar to family parties on such occasions. Mr. Whiteside had aged. Mrs. Collins thought, and Mrs. Whiteside's bonnet looked real shabby. Martha was there too, wearing her wedding-dress, a brown silk not half so pretty as Bessie's silver gray. Her husband brought up the rear, carrying the baby. It wasn't likely hie lordship would ever do such. a thing as that, Mrs. Collins reflected with a smile. But she was very ' affable and condescending to the Whitesides and told them in tones which she tried to make as little exultant as possible, that Bessie would be Lady Martindale in less than a week now. At the sound. of the name, a gentleman who had been approaching, scanning the houses as he walked, now drew near more rapidly:.
"Mr. Celina, I believe P' he said, pausing be- side her.

"Yes, sir," said Mrs. Collins, taking her arms off the gate, and becoming a woman of business at once. He had come about rooms most likely. Ile looked a nice gentleman, elderly and quiet, and Mrs. Collins reflected that though the drawing and dining room floors were occupied, the top back bedroom was free, and when the wedding was over, she would give up her own little parlour as she had often done before. "I come from Lord Martindale," said the gentle- man. "I am his man of business—my name is Hook_ He has commissioned me to talk over cer- tain little matters relating to his marriage with your daughter." "Will you step in, sir, please ?" enquired Mrs. Collins, smoothing her apron a little nervously. This elderly gentleman spoke gravely and looked at her oddly. She wondered what he had come to say. Mr. Hook took possession of the arm-chair which she pushed forward for him on entering the parlour, and looked at her for a moment or two, clearing his throat as though he found it difficult to begin. "You will naturally like to know," he said at last, "something about the provision which his lordship has made for your daughtet in case of his death."

"I never thought about it," returned Mrs. Col- lins simply, "at least I reckoned his lordship wouldn't ever let my garl come to want." The lawyer inclined his head, and proceeded to enumerate certain settlements of a very generous nature which had it appeared been drawn up for the benefit of the future Lady Martindale. Mrs. Collins was both astonished and grateful. When she had loudly and repeatedly expressed hergratification Mr. Hook proceeded "Now the question remains of your future, Mrs. Collins. Lord Martindale is anxious to make suit- able provision for you." He looked away but not before he had seen the wonYau start and stiffen herself.

"I am much obliged to his lordship, I am sure," she said coldly, "but he's no need to do anything of that kind. I've always been accustomed to do for myself and I'm thankful to say as I've always done well. His lordship has no need to trouble about me." "Well, but you see, Mrs. Collins' things are al- tered now. The mode of life which was right and becoming before is not suitable for Lady Martin- dale's mother—"
"You mean," interposed Mrs. Collins, looking at him sharply with her shrewd, keen eyes. "You mean as his lordship objects to my letting apart- ments P"

"Well, you see," replied Mr. Hook persuasively, "it isn't—ah—quite the right thing now. Circum- stances alter cases you see. Lord Martindale natur- ally doesn't quite like it. That was why," he added still more insinuatingly, "he commissioned me to make a—little proposal to you. He thought if he found you a nice house with some grounds perhaps and a—a" little conservatory you know. It would be more comfortable and more suitable for you than staying on here. lam sure this house will be too large for you if you gave up taking lodgers and I daresay it is cold in the winter. Now Lord Martindale was thinking if you went South—there are charm- ing villas to be had on the south coast—at Pen- zance for instance--I am sure you would like Pen- , zance, Mrs. Collins. it is a most delightful place." Mrs. Collins drew a long breath and looked hard at the lawyer, the colour slowly mounting in her face the while. The man's eyes fell; he could not brook that direct, questioning gaze. "His lordship wants to get rid of me," said Mrs. Collins. "I didn't think it of him. He had a mother himself—he didn't ought to take my gurl away from me:" Never in all his days perhaps had Mr. Hook been called upon to perform so unpleasant a task; he had undertaken many difficult bits of business before in the service of the noble family, of which Lord Mar- tindale was now the chief represents tive, but lie would rather have dealt with an army of importunate creditors than face this honest, straightforward, hard-working woman. But he stuck to his colours gallantly. "There is no use in beating about the bush," he said, "you have guessed the truth, Mrs. Collins. Lord Martindale feels that your presence here so near Martin Towers, is awkward, very awkward. Your daughter will naturally want to visit you often. You have many relations and friends here— very getod.pee_ple, _if am sure, _Eery excelle_nt.pepple.

div.head: EXAMINER FRI, Y MAY 2 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRI, Y MAY 2 1902

but not or claw to Ivllith—your (Mug-Eta will henceforth belong. It would be undesirable for her to be thrown among them. His lordship wishes m fact that her connection with this place should be broken altogether." "He don't know my girl," said Mrs. Collins de- fiantly. "She is not of that make—she'll not be put upon. She'll come here if she's a mind." "That is just the point," said the lawyer, draw- ing in his breath with a sucking sound, and rubbing his knees meditatively. ".1 think Lord Martindale anticipated there would be some little difficulty on that score. For this reason, Mrs. Collins, he is anxious that you should look upon this matter as en- tirely confidential. It is not at all desirable that your daughter should know anything about it. Now calm yourself, my dear Mrs. Collins pray calm yourself. Look at the matter quietly and seriously. No doubt your daughter's marriage to Lord Martin- dale is a niece of extraordinary—in fact I may say unprecedented good fortune. You see yourself that, in addition to raising her to a position which she can never have dreamed of attaining, he has provided for her, both during his lifetime, and in the event of his death, in a most handsome and most generous manner. He is moreover--I can speak with auth- ority for I have known him all his life—of a kind- hearted and affectionate disposition • his wife will be happy as well as prosperous. They are deeply attached to each other, and if any—ah—hitch were to occur, now, it would be a very great pity." "Au," said Mrs. Collins, "it's all true, sir, what you say, but I can't think my Bessie would like me to be treated so. She always thought a deal of her mother, my Bessie did, and .1 can't think she could make herself happy if she knew his lordship thought so little of me.'

"Tut, tut," said Mr. Hook, "you make a mis- take, Mrs. Collins—a very great mistake. I assure you Lord Martindale has the very highest respect for you. He told me so with his own lips. 'I am most anxious,' he said, to do everything in my power for Mrs. Collins. I feel that my wife's mother has a claim on me which I cannot disregard.' " I never wanted to have no claims on his lord- ship," interrupted the poor woman, firing up. "I never looked to him for anything. I know very well I am not his equals, and don't wish to put myself forward in no way. If his lordship thinks as I'd expect to e invited to Martin Towers when there wim (ornpany or that,. he's very much mistaken. But I (lid think as I might go and see rny Bessie sometimes when they was alone—l'd ha' liked to ha' seen my daughter's 'ome f—but I suppose his lord- ship wouldn't fancy my coming if ho 's set on takin' her off me."

" heally, Mrs. Collins, I am quite certain that his Lordship has no such idea," responded the lawyer hastily ; he could scarcely bear to look at those hon- est, pleading eyes, the transitory fire in which was now dimmed by tears. "He said nothing what- ever about taking your daughter away from you, and I' ye no doubt will be very glad to welcome you to Martin Towers from time to time." It must be owned that M. Hook made this last statement en- tirely on his own responsibility. " What he feels," wmt on, " is that it is most desirable that your should adapt herself to her new position. The sool:ei ie breaks with old associations the bet- ter, and the less she is tempted to return to them the easier will be her task. Now, Mrs. Collins, I appeal to you, as a sensible woman, and a good mother, to help his Lordship instead of hindering him. What has been your aim and object all your life, if not to promote the happiness and well-being of your daughter? If you put obstacles in the way of his Lordship's plan, the married life of the young couple will be very likely be over shadowed from the be- ginning, by bickerings and discontent, if.—" he paused for a moment, and then continued, looking fixedly at Mrs. Collins the while—" if the marriage takes place at all." . - .
" You mean," cried Mrs. Collins hotly, "that unless my gun l consents to give up her mother, he'll throw her over ?"

"I don't say so —exactly. Lord Martindale did not contemplate the possibility of your refusing- to comply with his wish. But I think—ah---if diffi- culties arose, that his Lordship would be much puzzled how to act—very much puzzled." "Then he isn't worth tuppence !" cried Mrs. Collins scornfully and emphatically. "I do not agree with you," returned Mr. Hook, "and I think you will find that your daughter would not agree with you either. I will venture to wager that your daughter considers Lord Martindale worth a deal more than twopence." Mrs. Collins was silent : the words pierced her heart like a knife. They were true ; her Bessie made a deal of his Lordship! " Lord Martindale is practically throwhig himself upon your mercy," pursued the lawyer, eagerly fol- lowing up the impression he had made. "For your daughter's sake you know, Mrs. Collins--for your daughter's sake, he relies upon your discretion. He quite realises that if you were to consult her the whole matter would probably fall through, and therefore he hopes that in her interests you will keep the proposed arrangements a secret." "If I've got to leave my 'ome, I must tell her," said Mrs Collins hoarsely. "I've never kept a secret from Bessie in her life—she's the only child I've got —she's all I've got !" "Well, well, it is a great sacrifice no doubt—a very great sacrifice; but it is for her sake after all —you don't want to deprive her of her good luck. So you'll be very cautious, Mrs. Collins. I should say nothing at all to your daughter for the present, and then afterwards, after the marriage you know" —with an airy wave of his hand—" you might just write and tell her that as it is no longer necessary for you to work for your living you have settled to give up your house and remove to—somewhere— where there is a more genial climate." Mrs. Collins stood silent for a moment looking straight before her with dry burning eyes and squeez- ing her toil-roughened hands closely together. "I have lived in this houEe," she said at last, "ever since I was married. I chose the papers and paint myself, and I had a tiash-house built, and I planted all the flowers in the garden, and Bessie she was born here. I never looked to leave this place. My grandfather was Mayor of this town once—all my family has lived here for years and years." She paused with a little gasp, but continued as a new thought struck her: "And my furniture is that heavy and old-fash- ioned, it'll be a hard job to shift it." "As to that," put in the lawyer quickly, "Lord Martindale will see that you are put to no expense. He is anxious as I tell you to make a settlement—" "I'll not take a penny," interrupted Mrs. Collins fiercely. "I'll not sell my gurl. If I did such a thing at all, Wad be for her sake because I want her to be 'appy ; but I don't say as how I'll do it— there's things as I don't think a body can do and oughtn't to be asked to do. I'll think on it—and I'll drop you a line to-morrow. That's best." Mr. Hook consulted his watch. "I could go back by the seven o'clock train," he said, " and it is only half-past four now. I will take a little walk and come back in two hours. Pctimps by that time you will have made up your . He went out, shakims ;101111 as he walked away, and muttering to 11;1114'1 t'.. these unequal marri- ages brought about a peat al of misery. (To le Concluded.)

Last year Glasgow had its great Exhibition, and this year Wolverhampton is the chosen site Of one almost as big and important. Those who only know the town from the railway do not realise what &dna place it is architecturally, as the stations are placed amongst its mean streets, and on Thursday, when the Duke and Duchess of Con- naught went to the Midlands to open the Exhibition, it was a revelation to many of the visitors who flocked down to the ceremony. There is no question but that the Mayor and Corporation of this old town, which was founded in 964 by Wrilfrena, and the Exhibition Committee have to be most warmly congratulated upon the success of their efforts, which have entailed a great deal of hard work and enterprise. The architecture of the Exhibition, which is one of Arts and Industries, cannot be classed under any particular heading, being a rather fantastic combination of Spanish Renaissance and Byzantine with an Oriental touch over the whole: but it must be pro- nounced very striking and effective with its domes' towers and minarets of dazzling white and buildings of imitation marble with cupolas of dead silver and bright bronze. One of the most striking features is the great horseshoe portico which faces the entrance gates, and this design is repeated in other places. The grounds are thirty-two acres in extent and are
WHO OPENED THE 'WOLVERHAMPTON EXHIBITION ON THURSDAY.

lit throughout by electricity, which has been one of the most important and growing industries of Wolverhampton during the last fifteen or twenty years. The big Industrial Hall contains not only local exhibits, such as locks and safes, silver goods, specimens of the cycle trade etc., • but wares from all over the United Kingdom of three hundred or more firms. India and Japan are also represented, while Canada boasts a pavilion of her own, under the dome of which rises a huge trophy of the agri- riltural products of that Colony. The Machinery Hall,,,at the entrance of which stands a colossal statu6 of Industry, contains plant and machinery upon a gigantic scale, as is naturally expected from a town where electric Ilkipparatus is such a leading feature. Bootraaking, a very old industry in Wolverhampton, printing and book- binding wilt be shown on he latest machines from America. In addition, there is a magni- ficent concert hall, in which gymnastic displays will also be held, restaurants, band- stands, and many side shows; while at the Art Gallery in the town a very striking loan exhibi- tion of pictures w‘ill be run synchronously. Altogether, the Exhibition has all the features of prosperity, and should be successful in paying off the debt on the Free Library, for which object the profits will be set aside.

Rumours continue to be rife about the great Atlantic combine, and great uneasiness is ex- pressed upon every hand at this latest move on the part of Mr. Pierpont Morgan who, it is also reported, recently made an offer for the London and South-Western Railway en bloc, which was, however, refused. T here is no question but that there is a great scheme afloat in the States to obtain a strong control in British matters by regulating our trade and our • food supply so far as America is concerned, and there is no doubt that, unless very active steps are taken to foil the plans of the millionaires, we shall find our- selves in a tvery dangerous posi- tion in a few years' time. It is obvious to all that Mr, Pierpont Morgan, whose name appears at the foretront of each new Brob- dingnagian pro- posal, i s not working single- handed, as no man could pos- sibly have con- ox OF THE AMERICAN MILLION. trol of such vast AIRES IN TUE GREAT SUIPPING TRUST. wealth as is
JOHN DAVIDSON ROCKEFELL ER

ideas require for C ompletion. Amongst his chief supporters the foremost is Mr. J. D. Rockefeller, of the Standard Oil Trust, who probably represents the biggest block of avail- able capital in the world, and is unquestionably one of the astutest and hardest-headed of all the Yankee capitalists. The questions asked in the House lately with reference to the Shipping Trust show that many members are alive to the dangers of the position, and the grave menace to British supremacy, and it is hoped that some way of preventing this gradual absorption of our interests will be found. The firm stand of the Cunard line. and Mr. Ismay's denial with reference to the White Star Line are two hopeful signs in the outlook

There are a few people who are so generally popular that their party is of little account in the opinion even of their opponents, and foremost amongst these is Lord CilarleA Beresford, who, since the days of the bombardment of Alexan- dria, has been a national idol. Besides this, though a staunch Unionist, he Admiral is by no means a bigot in his opinions, and is a man who it is widely felt has a distinct claim to a seat in the House of Commons on account of his opinion on naval matters, and his experience in the senior service. Hence it was a surprise to nobody that LORD CHARLES HERESPORD
st EW MEMBER FOR WOOLWICH.
H. A. LAW

NEW MEMBER FOR DONEG the Liberals decided not to run a bandidate against him at Woolwich, though at one time a contest was suggested on behalf of the Labour Party. However, when the time of nomination came, Mr. O'Donnelrs name was not put forward, and it was seen that they had decided not to fight a hopeless election, especially as they were hampered for want of funds. Lord Charles Beresford is most enthusiastically welcomed by members of all shades of opinion, as it is thought that his presence will tend towards practical naval reform in many matters in which an expert's opinion is needed and in which little additional expense will be involved. Another new Member of Parliament is Mr. H. A. Law. the Nationalist representative for Donegal, who has come to swell the ranks of the Irish at Westminster. He belongs to a well-known Iris political family, his father having been Lord Chancellor of Ireland.

Lacrosse, the old game of the Red Indian and tfib national game of Canada, is not very well known in England in general, althouTh there are by now a large number of clubs which play matches amongst themselves both in the North and in the South, and have formed an Association under which con- tests for supremacy are held upon " league " lines, The game, however, has never been very popular, although it contains many features of interest and calls for a combination of skill and endurance. But this spring those interested in its development have considered it in a sufficiently advanced state to

justify a visit from a representative team from Canada under the auspices of the Duke of Argyll and others and the visit of the King and the Prince of Wales ..to Lord's last Saturday to watch the game between the Duke's team and the Canadian visitors should give the game a great social fillip. The latter won very easily by 11 goals to 3, outplaying the Englishmen at every ,point of the game, but, con- sidering the comparative newness of its introduction into England, a couple of decades ago at the most, and the limited conditions

div.p: 4' LACROSSE " AT LORD'S LAST SATURDAY, WIT-

/of development, this is not to be wondered at and the exhibition must be considered a satisfactory one. Saturday, also, saw the completion of the Football Cup after the draw of the preceding, week, Sheffield United beating Southampton by two goals to one after a hard game. As usual, much discur.sion and dispute has arisen as to the respective merits of the two Clubs; but it is generally thought that the better team won.

The music-halls promise to be very lively during the Coronation season, and at present there are many good new songs winning their way into popularity. Foremost amongst these is Mr. George Robey's "Prehistoric Man" song, which scored an instantaneous success, and is one of the best he has ever sung during his career. It is the great " draw " at the halls at which he is engaged and comes in for encore after encore every night. Last Saturday was an important evening in the theatrical year, as Sir Henry Irving made his re-appearance at the Lyceum ,in Faust after his American tour. He was most enthusiastically wel- comed by a packed audience, many of whom had been waiting for twelve hours at the pit and gallery entrances, and there is no doubt that his personal popularity has not waned in his absence. It is seventeen years since Sir Henry Irving first pro- duced Faust but his acting in the rile of Mephistopheles is as virile and as finished as ever. In those days, Miss Ellen Terry made a sensation as "Margaret," but now she has been superseded by Miss Cecelia Loftus better known to the public as Miss Cissie Loftus, who has fought her way up from the boards of the music halls and her famous mimicry to the front rank of s,:rious acting. The playing of the new leading lady at the Lyceum was certainly disappointing in places and uneven, but in the dungeon scene Miss Loftus rose to a great height and showed that her powers

GEORGE RO THZ FAMOUS COMEDIAN AS A " PREHISTORIC MAN." limp not bean over-rated. Mr. Stanford, thE new Faust, was rather weak, but on the whole the production was a triumph and marks a most interesting epoch in the annals of the Lyceum. Never has His Majesty shown greater activity in his patronage of the drama, and immediately upon his return to town he paid a visit to 4 Chinese Honeymoon, which has passed its 200th performance and is going very well, while on Saturday, by visiting the Alhambra to see the Japanese ballet, he made his first appearance in a music hall since his accession to the throne.

The inhabitants of Folkestone have taken a lively interest in a well-known and respected inhabitant said o have been lost in his own house for ten months. The " Folkestone Chronicle and Observer " publishes a des- cription of the affair. The house wee 33, Gladstone- road, where a representative of the paper went to verify the facts.

Said he, addressing Mr. Ftancis, " Are you the gentle- man who lost himself for the period of ten months ?" I. That is quite eorrect." "Do you mind telling me the circumstances ?" " Oh, not at all. My age is thirty-eight. lam an

,s,, of Folkestone. The man who was lost for ten months in his own house. engine-fitter, and I work mostly for big contractors. In 1395 I was e ngaged at the Manchester Ship Canal,wlaere in an accident I received a slight injury with a Mail piece of iron on the back of my head. My mate was killed at my side. Interesting Wedding at.Limm.

A large congregaiion assemSied in Lymm Parish Church on Tuesday morning, to witness the marriage of Dr Henry Ambroselßurrowes, of Chureh. Green, Lymm, and Miss Nora Eleanor Brabszon, second daughter of Dr Brabezon, M.D.. J.P., of Brook House, Lymm. The officiating clergy were the Rev G B Thurston, rector of Lymm, and the Rev F C Bozmati, curate. The bride, who looked charming in a dress of pale grey tweed, with black chiffon hat, was attended by her sister, Miss Frances Brabazon, who wore pale grey and grey chiffon hat, trimmed with piak roses, and was given away by bar father. The best man was Mr James Lister. On the conclusion of the ceremon) the bells rang ont a merry peal, and appropriate wedding music was played by Mr P W Maniere, the organist. Num-roue well-wishers gave the bride and bride- groom a hearty reception as they walked down the churchyard to their carriage, and the scene, with the brilliant sunshine and the flags gaily flying, was an exceedingly pretty one. Dr Brabszen (whose daughter has been connected with the Sun- day school and other institutions belonging to the Pariah Church) kindly gave the boys a treat to celebrate the occasion and Pr Burrowes gave the girls a good tea. Carriages were lent by Captain Groves, Mr T P Norris, and Mrs Grundy.

A Warrington Cyclist in Trouble -at Ashton Thomas Tabernacle, a boiler maker, of 77. Marsh House-lane, Warrington, was charged with using obscene language in Gerard-street,Ashton-in-Maker- field, at a quarter past twelve on buuday morning the 13th of April.— Inspector Palmer said that the defendant along with two other members of the Padgate Cycling Club came to Ashton some time- on the evcning previous to the offence being committed. They stayed there until a late hour and after closing time, made a round of the public - houses in the district. All three - demanded admittance, but they were refused. Ultimately,shortly after twelve o'clock, they arrived' at the Cress Keys Inn, Gerard-street, the occupants of which house bad - retired to bed. Defendant commenced to Create a disturbance, and the son of the licensee got up to the bedroom windbw,and said he would clear them away. He came down, and fulfilled his promise. Defendant with the other* went some distance away and Tabernacle com- menced to use obscene language. He (the inspector then came up and told defendant be would be rs ported.—Defendant now said it was a "frivolous case." He had been assaulted by somenne connected with one of the public-houses' He did not remem- bet using the language imputed to him.—Defendant was fined 108 and costs.

Shortly befere Friday midnight, the death occurred of o.mncillor George Plumpton, son of the late tfr rhorn is Piunaptoo, iormerly of Farnworto and Wirriugtou Oaring his ia:t illness, Coiju- cillor was confined to his bed about a week. He caught a chill while attendiniz the Board of Trade inspsction of the new tramway system Bronchitis and pneumonia supervened, to which lie succumbed at his residence, 125, L vely- lane. his wife pre-deceased him some years ago and he leaves four sons —fierbert, George, Frank and ';tephen. the last-named son was summoned from Lindon by telegraph and arrived in Warring- ton by the early morning train, just a few hours after his father's death. Dr Illsby was is medical attendant. Immediately on the receipt of the news of Councillor Piumptou's death, the flags at the : Town kiall and the Liberal Club were lowered half- mast.

Councillor Plumpton was a self made mon. After working for some time at Lynam he returned to Warrington and assisted his father in a small tool and file manufacturing business: Ultimately he became the proprietor of it.. whic by dint of perseverance and usinsss agility he increased to one of no mean itnportance• He firuly es- tablished th /Albion Tool and File Works in Leices- ter-street, and the produ!tions of the works are well—known far and wile. Ore the 15tn June,lB9l, Ir Piumpton segurecl a Seat on the Warring, on Town Council after a spirited contest in Whitecross Ward. The election wao to supply a casual vacancy caused by the promotion of the late Mr E Greenall to the position of Alderman. Mr A Yoods was the Conservative candidate but Mr Plumpton won MI seat for Liberalism by 83 votes ,n the let Novem- ber of the same 'oar, Mr Plumpton was called upon to fight once more for municipal honours, his opponent on this occasion being a resident in the ward and a mole t strongsr candidate. in the person of Mr William Bellian. Nevertheless Mr Plimpton retained the seat by a mojorify of 49 votes. and was cow inuously in office until the time of his death, he haviag represente I the ward for over ten years. He was the seni ir councillor, and according to the existing arrangement as to seniority, entitled to the ilext, vacant. Aldermanic seat. Ile was a member or tme Street Improvement anti Lighting C mimi!tee,Health Committee, Paving and Sewerage Comm nee, Fire Engine Committee and Tramways Commia,ee. He was regular in his attendance at the conundlee and Council meetings and took a keen interest in all municipal , affairs. Tho imprOved paving and lighting of st,reets and passages in Whitecross Ward ii largely due to the persistence with which he advocated such improvements. Sankey Brook and its foul emanations claimed his especial atten- tion and he raisod his voice in pro'est again and again. Ile was deeply interested in the inaugnra- tion of the tramway system and it was whilst accompanying the members on the trial journey, shortly after his recovery from an illness, that he contracted a cold which culminated in his death. tie was a staunch Liberal in politics and at the last general election be took a prominent part in supporting the candidature of Mr A Crosfield He was one of the vice-presidents of the Liberal Club and one of its most v dued members. He wor- shipped at Wycliffe Congregational Church,and was a regular attender at the services, lie was a liberal contributor to the new memorial buildings.

Interesting Letter.

TO THE EDITOR OF "THE WARRINGTON EXAHINER." Dear Sir,—The last time you were good enough to afford me the opportunity to discuss political questions in your columns, the all absorbing topic of the war was my theme; and in all conscience the events which led up to that war and its consequences have been enough to give us pause. But now ether events engage atter.- tion in the political world, and cad to mind a saying of our old friend Mr McMinnies, " Gave a Tory Govern- ment rope enough and it will bang itself." The present situaisun appears to be a wry interesting illustration of that theore.n. Same of us,it is true,may not greatly distress ourselves at the prospect of Tories committing political suicide, but it is our duty to protest, and we Liter tes do protest most strongly against the damage they are doing to the trade and commerce of the coun- try, and the way in which they are undermining the welfare of the masses of the people. . .

... ~ . . In criticising these things the difficulty is selection. Liberals at the present moment have to centend not with the lack but the abundance of subjects which call, and call urgently, for ere:lei:sm. To attempt ,a survey in a single letter would be, as our homely phrase , has it, to try to" Get a quart into a pint pot,"—a feat which is . understood to be practicable only north of the border. 1 One may however summarise the situation by saying that this Government has, put the hands of the political clock:back thirty -two yetrs aWe are in many respects in exactly the position we were in in the year 1869 or 1870. It was in 1859 we abolished the last remnant of the iniquitous Corn Laws that inflinced such aggravated suffering upon the people. It was in 1870 we fought the battle for the existence of School Beards that we are , I now practically4called upon to fight again. This year our National debt has reached the enormous sum of £800,000.000, just the amount at which it stood in 1870 Thus we have in the past three years wiped out the re- suit of all the efforts made during thirty-two yeers to reduce the weight of that national millstone. These ! reactionary taxes and reactionary measures, or more properly speaking, the general trend of events of ! late years remind us forcibly enough of John Stuart Mill', wise aphorism, " 'the price of liberty is eternal vigilance." And not tbe least significant example is the debate in tbe House of Commons on the treatment of Cartwright reported in the papers this very day. We are reminded too that the teacaings of the Mauchester School, of Cobden, Bright and Gladstone are still of immense economic value. IThe most vital question before us now is still the issue of peace or war, and we all;hope the negotiations for peace will be conducted ia a broad-minded, generous spirit so that as far as poesible we may be able to build up in South Africa, not a second Ireland, but a prosperous and contented Colony. A little more patience and a little more of the" give and take" spirit three years ago would almost certainly have averted war ; die not let us fall let-) the same error with regard to peace. I am not goingeto traverse the old debatable ground in discussing the pros and cons of the war and the events preceding it. But it is as well to bear in mind *Mat the war occurred not because we bad to face the alternative of, on the one hand keuckline under to the Boers, or, on thetother maintaining our natural predominance in South Africa, but because,—thanks to our impossible and indeed shameless diplomacy—we, in effect, refused to accept as a settlement of the question concessions which, as Mr Chamberlain himself admitted in reply to Sir Edward Clark in the House of Commons, amounted to nine-tenths of our original demand. How many of us are there now, how many wealthy capitalists are there, even on the Rand, who, if we had the time over , again would may the last tenai was worth all this bitter work and intense suffericg, this fearful expenditure and the further expensive legacy of hatred which is be- queathed us? I woeld like to draw attention to the enormous cost of this war. It was, we remember,to cost ten millions; to be a " military promenade." It has cost already £200,000,000; it is costing us three times as much a year as Me Crimean War cost us e it is costing nearly twice as much a year as the great wars against Napoleon— when we were fighting the whole world for some time; it is casting six times the amount a year we spent on the war with the American Colonies, now the United States. As I have said, we have, ever since 1815, been striving to reduce our National Debt. We do not pay our way as well as fifty years ago. War is a costly thing, and science is year by year making it more coetly. Our war expenditure (apart from the cost of actual hostilities) is mountine up year by year without our being ;in a stronger position than before. Other nations are seffering in the same way. Surely common sense and business prudence demand that we should do all in our power to encourage the settlement of inter- national disputes by the principles of right in place of might ; by arbitration in place of the sword. But the question that is uppermost in our minds just now must be the Man:whereby, this reactionary Govern- ment seeks to ,raise additional revenue. we are told that extra Tea Duty, the extra Tobacco Duty,cthe extra Beer Duty; theVxtra Spirit Unties ; the new Sugar Duty : the new Coal Tax ; and the new Bread Tax are all war taxes and the people must pay for their " mafficking." We shall have to pay the bill undoubt- edly, but we are not going to allow the Government to ride off thus easily. The maiises were not able to study the causes of the war ; they took the word of their Government as literally true when that Government assured them that the war was !just and unavoidable If any tnie dared to put the other side of the question, he was denounced by the members cf that Government as a " Pro-Boer," or in other false and epprobrious , names. And again the new taxes are taxes for a war that was declared over twenty months ago. No, a Government that obtained office on false pretences, cannot now accuse the people of participation, and shift the responsibility on to them. But yet again, these taxes are not "War Taxes." They are intended to be permanent. Indeed if war stopped to-marrow they could not be remitted unless we substi- tuted new isources of revenue. We are at the parting of the ways, and must either return to that system of "Protection" which our fathers found to be such an evil and abandcn the system of Free Trade which they inau- gurated and which has done so much for the country ; or else, We must resort to sOll3O new source of direct taxation. It has been found by experience that to put duties upon a number of articles is not the best way to raise revenue ; that the fewer there are of such duties the more they and the other great sources of revenue yield. Thanks to our system of raising revenue in ,tbe past the wealth of the country has greatly developed and that wealth has been taxeed through the Income Twee; then again, through the Death Duties ; but there is another form of accumulated wealth that has not yet been tapped—the enormous value added to the land of this country, especially in our towns—by the presence and industry of the people. This value is created by the people not by the landowners, and ought to be taxed for the pecple instead of our having taxes upon food. It is not as though there were no alternative to the bread tax ; we must tax the land values poured into the laps of men, who, to use Mr Chamberlain's Biblical expression, " toil not, neither do they spin," It is impossible to imagine a more cruel or foolish tax than the tax on bread,Ou this ar:icle alone it will mean that a workman will have to pay about fasten- pence a week at least. But the grain tax enters into so many different articles that the amount paid in bread is only a dortion of the taxation it will entail upon the worker. lam told by the aecretary of the Financial Reform Association that when the rise in the various articles, or what is the same, the failing off in quantity or quality, is taken into account, it will be foued tha while the Go :ernmert has increased the Income Tax upon the rich by one penny, it has imposed taaati, xi equal to an Income Tax at one shilling upon the man with a pound a week. A book has recently been published on " Poem ty "in York by Mr llowntree and he has shown that about thirty per cent of the population does not even at the pre. tsent low prices offood, get enough to eat to keep them in he degree of he.dth necessary to allow them to do a proper day's cork. Putting it upon these low grounds, we perceive whet a piece of legielative folly this bread tax is. Cheap food, cheap raw materials, and cheap labour are the life blond of cur trade. In this, the twentieth century, we ought to be devising the best means of increasing the food and comforts of the peopM not seeking by taxation to reduce them. That, in this age of sciecce and invention,nearly one third of the people should not have enough to eat, is a crying die- erne to our vaunted civilisation. Well may Str Henry Yowler speak of the meanness of this tax. Ale's serious matter, but still a point well worth ccnsidering is the endless trade disorganisation this tax will mean. The importation of flour and grain now is a huge trade; but now for months before the introduction of the budget, the corn trade viii te disorganised. The mer- chants will not know whether tato tax is to remain the same, to be abolished, or to be increased. They will not know whether to buy or to refrain from buying. Be it noed also that we are going to destroy a growing , export trade in flour, which trade will go to the United States new. Rice is taxed, and by raising the price of i rice, we limit its consumption ; that is we inflict an ' k injury upon the rice growers of eßritish Eest India and 1 Burmeh, our Own Colonists. . Lencashire took the lead in demanding the repeal of the Corn Jaws and Liverpool continued the agitation until the SO called " Registratien Duty " was repealed. This was net done by Mr Lowe because he had a tut- plus with whica be did not know what to do ; the eboU- tion of the duty was part of a car -dully thouebt out scheme. I am confident Lancashire will once attain teke the lead in demanding the repeal of these unjust taxes upon food. As in the stupid and foothill revival of coercion in Ireland, ac in eduziational matte, s; en in this bread tax the Tories have at laet come out into the open and shown themselves in their true colours-- Faithfully yours. April 25th,1902.
A. IL CHOSFIELD.

div.head: MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS AND PZ.R-
div.p: MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS AND PZ.R-
SALTS, LIMITED.
More Insinuations in the Bankruptcy
Court.

' In the Manchester Bankruptcy Caurt on Monday, the examination in bankruptcy Jf Harold Ford, promoter at a company called Persalts, Limited, for the creataneut of sewage, was continued before Mr Reaistrar Atkinson. It was stated on a former occasion that Mr S Norbury Williams had contributed £lOO, aid was to have taken an active part in the management of One Of tho com- panies in which Mr Flrd was interested. The Official Receiver (Mr C J Dibb) asked if Mr Williams did not sign a contract for the purchase of certain works for £2,700. The debtor answered in the affirmative. "Do you know," Mr Dibb next asked, " whether he is being held liable for the completion of that contract?" The debtor replied: "My information is that he is." It was stated that Mr Williams had been allowed a sum of money for ills expenses in travelling about on the com- pany's business. He had been, it was said, two or three times to Glasgow. Mr Clobbett (who appeared for creditors): What did he go for 7—T./see the works. We know he is an expert in Corporation expenditure, but what do s he knew about a syatern for the treatment of sewage, or sewage works P—Well, he very soon mas- tered this question, in my opinion. Why should you employ a gentleman who is not a civil engineer, nor a valuer, nor, apparently, in any business connected with the treatmefia of sewage, and pay him £2O to go tray Ailing about the country to look at places ?—Tate idea was that his name on the prospec- tus as managing director would cause the company to be well aubiciibd for.

Then was the £2O a sort of tiz-bit " for him ?—He must have his expenses. Naturally, that Is what peop'e are always sating. You thought £2O would tend to get his name on the pros- pectus?—He would not have taken it. I Go Rot say he would, but I ask, did you not think it would tend to get his name on the prosp.!ctu,?-0,1, yes, I thought that. Mr Batty (for the debtor) You do net suggest that Mr Williams has not absolutely accounted ior every item he has received?-oh, no. .

What he received wai simply out-of-pocket ex- penses, and as tar as you know he spent them in travehing in the interests of the Gompanv ?—That is s But as a matter of fact yo 1 CORSiI e end rol had secured his name for the proposA syndicate ?—Ye;. It is a fact you Zot his name on tho draft prospectus ? —Yes, I got his signature in writing. The prospectus indicated you wore the person floating the company ?—Yes. Mr Bstty said the debtor had done himself great in- justice at his previous examinations, and it was neces- sary to correct some of his vatements.

It was agrPed that Mr Bitty should prepare it otatr- meat and submit it to the o!fi )ial It-neiv-r, and if ap- proved it could then be added t ) trie paper.' in the cts The examinaton was adjourned to the 2e4 June. LET rER FROM MR. WILLIAMS. " COMPANY FLO PATION EXPERIENCE." _ .
To the E lor of the "Manchester Evening News."

Sir,—l notice that my name his again been -mentione and in a very unpleasant way, in connection with the bankruptcy examination of Mr Harold Ford at Manches- ter on Monday. lam compelled now tv say, in my own defence, that it was at the request of a near relative of the bankrupt that I conrented to make inquiries as to the pa eats which Mr Ford was propasing to purchase This relative was to b-come a director of the suggest.d company. I accordingly made exhaustive inquiries which occupied a long time. I notice that the bankrupt attributes the failure of his enterprise to my delay. But I was determined not to proceed instil every inquiry was complete. Experts and chemists take their own time. However, at last, I had obtained reports from sures of our most distinguished men, and was satisfied that the patents in question accomplished , all that was claimed for them,,and resulted in products which were unequalled by any other process. This occupied some months ; doubtless the bankrupt would have liked it to have been finish,d in a week. He says I 1" spoilt it by delay." I reply that it was not delay, , but a proper salutary caution. The gentlemen connected with the matter were all inm of the highest honour and well known. P,rsonally, I had nothing whatever to do with Ford's £4OO, nor with, the way in which Ford had agreed to compensate the four gentlemen who paid the money to him. I h ton never heard till now that Ford we to receive 180 £1 share.. What Ido know is that I have received from the bankrupt ray net travelling expenses (some £1.3 in all), and not another penny in any shape The dealt ' prospectus was drawn up entirely by Ford. The pro- ducts of the Patents are not equ died in England to- day. The business was a thoroughly honer,honourable one. If there was any delay, it was through a scrupu- lous deire that ev,-r v point should be verified before the matter was made public. I have written the fore- going with great pain and rolultanee. I hope it will not be necessary to say any more, but I cannot allow my name and my honour to be trifled with in a court of law or anywhere else.—Yours, &e. , S. NORBURY WILLIAMS. 75, Shakespeare-street, Manchester,April 29,1902.

He saw the child last June and it was then pefectly healthy but covered with lice. div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
EARLFBTOWN POLICF. V. EARLEsTowN TRiDEDIEN.

At Harlestown on Tuesday evening a match was played between the local police and tradesmen, the proceeds of which were in aid ot the proposed Coronation Horse Ambu- lance for Harlestown. Alter a time the Police forced their way down, and with a good shot Mellor drew first blood for the "men in blue" Fitzgerald scored the first and second goals for the Tradesmen. Half-time: Tradesmen 2 goals, Police 1 goal. On resuming, the Tradesmen returned to work very quickly, and Singleton scored again. Mellor ran through with the second goal for the Police. Spence worked the ball up, and centred to Clarke. the latter passing back for Spence to score and equalise 'Singleton gave the Tradesmen the lead shortly after. The Police made great endeavours to get even, and Mellor was successful. Singleton scored again for the Tradesmen. Final : Tradesmen 5 goals, Police 4 goals
