div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
MAY 2nd 1902.

T lIE Parliamentary The Parliamentary machine, according to Mr Machine. BALFOUR, 19 still going badly. No franker confession of that could be regarded than his warning that the Commons may have to hold late sittings during the coming week. The object, of course, is that the most important of the new procedure rules may be brought to work on May sth, and that the Government may get the benefit of the increased appropriation of time. There are signs, indeed, that the Ministry is losing its spell over Parliament, and that, apart from the Irish difficulty, it finds the situation far from pleasant. The session began in the third week in January, or more than a fortnight earlier than the average date of opening. The Easter holdiday was cut down to the smallest possible limit, and it is proposed that tho same severe restriction shall occur at Whitsuntide ; and indeed, according to rumour, members will then have less than a week's % acation. Of course,there

will be a short break for the Coronation, but what is that compared with the announcement made at this early period that an autumn session is Inevitable. According to Mr BALFOUR'S own showing, the Governmeot started with a very modest programme, but in order to keep the ship going it is necessary to work the engines at what is practically their highest pressure. That strain is bound to tell on a H -me for whom the present members of the G.)vernment having, most of them, held continuous office since 189 G, have lost the interest of freshness. More than one Minister has acknowledged in conversation that he would he glad to be free of the responsibility, and Mr BRODRICK is becoming irritable and pettish. In these circumstances, the movement o set the new rules working is dictated by Mr. BALFOUR for reasons much stronger than personal

convenience. The progress so far has certainly been alarm- ingly slow. Even after the main propositions are adopted, there will be a great deal more to be done to the procedure rules. Although it has passed its principal stages, the Budget is still capable of giving some trouble; and the corn tax has alarmed town representatives and perplexed country ones. The Education Bill, like a magician's wand, has united the Liberal party, with the hearts of Mr. PERKS and Mr. LLOYD-GEORGE beating to tune in one honest indignation. It has stirred, too, that object of much satire—the Nonconformist conscience ; and offers us the pros- pect, if it be passed into law, of Mr. HUGH PRICE HUGHES resisting the rate-collector. It is certain to be fought in the House of Commons almost word for word,and Ar. BA.LFOUR cannot well drop it as he has so many before—the pressure from behind will prevent that. The Licensing Bill pre- aents fewer difficulties, but some of its features, especially the new restrictions on clubs, need careful consideration, because when once varied the law on that subject is not likely to be altered for some years to'eome, as regaris regis- tration. The Irish Land Bill is designed, with much skill and balance of thought, to meet what Mr. Wrxenala admits is an urgent and most melancholy evil, and, at the same time, to do justice as between landlord and ten- ant. It is a finely-conceived measure, whether or not it be practical. Appearances indi- cate that it wd.l have to be abandoned this session. Then there is the London Water Bill, which is apparently only out for an airing. Procedure, supply, licensing, and education, with a few small things, will make up the work to the -end of the year; and the House will be sitting close on to Christmas. Mr BALFOUR may well be anxious that there shall be some signs of despatch in the Government work, and that it shall be dis- tributed methodically. The results, at best, must be poor for the phenomenal amount of labour.

Lord SPENCER'S elec Lord Spencer and the • ti on as Leader of the Liberal Peers. Liberal party in the House of Lords, altholigh it was a foregone con- clusion does not lack interest on that account. The Red Earl" has passed through the experimental stage,having familiarised himself with the duties by acting as deputy for Lord Km BERLEY during the latter's illness. The new loader comes to his posi- tion as co-chief with Sir HENRY CAMPBELIrBAN- xEnmeN free from the annoyances of cross currents. Imperialists and Radicals, as it happens, hold him in equal regard, and there can be no doubt that he

will exert a powerful unifying influence over I the party. Lord SPENCER is exceedingly happy 'in his administrative record. As First Lord lof the Admiralty in a Liberal Government, he gave the first impetus to the movement of strengthening the Navy. As Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland, at a most critical moment in the history of the Liberal party, he gave his adhesion clearly and unequivocally to Mr. GiaansroNn's Home Rule proposals. Lord SPENCER is a man who forms his judgments slowly, but unless the conditions under which they are made change, they remain firm. Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bills are dead, but to the broad principle Ivhich they involve—that Ireland should be governed according to the wishes of its inhabitants—he holds as tenaci- ously as ever. Nobody can accuse him of little Englandism, or of any inclination to trim his views to meet the feeling of the moment. In many other ways he disarms prejudice. He is a generous landlord with a keen interest in agricultural pursuits. Unlike some landowners, he recognizes fully that property has its rights as well as its duties. His aristocratic environment has never had the effect of debilitat- ing his Liberalism. Only a few weeks ago he said that he rejoiced in the title of Radical. There is perfect accord between Lord SPENCER and Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANN/IR:AIN, and the two leaders may be expected to work in complete har- mony and thus help to consolidate the Liberal party. Finally, the Liberal peers may justly be proud tobo led by so chivalrous a leader as Earl SPENCER, than whom there is not a purer figure in our political life.

The cricket season has opened to find most of 1 the problems which have Seen perplexing devotees of the national game for the past few years still apparently no nearer solution. It is true that the M.C.C. has declared against the artificial wicket— that is, the wicket prepared other than by water and roller. But the problem of how to restore the I bowler to his former position as against the bats- man is not determined, and to all appearances will not be determined for some time. It has been proposed that the bowling crease shall be ' widened a foot each Way, and this question is to be considered by a general meeting of the M.C.C. ; but even if it is agreed upon the advantages will be rather of doubtful value, except in regard to one or two particular bowlers. A proposition which would do more to affect the general interest of cricket as a whole , is that regarding the extension of the " declare- , tion " rule. For many seasons past it has been amply demonstrated that if the increasingly great proportion of "draws "is to be checked captains must be given greater power with reference to " declaring "an innings. At present their power is limited yet it has been proved over and over again that the power to " declare " makes for a proper finish, and has done much to put a stop to the tendency fel. " draws," which is due to the in- creasing command of the bat over the ball on first-class wickets. It certainly does not seem unwise to suggest that, the operation of the rule having been so beneficial, it might now be ex- tended so as to give captains power in their dis- cretion to declare at any stage of the game.

An interesting project is before the Italian Parliament for a compulsory day of rest for work- men. Tne measure, introduced by the Labour representatives, indeed, goes further than our own now almost neglected Sabbath Day legisla- tion, in that it aims at securing for the employed an intermission of toil fer thirty-six hours conse- cutively, which must include Sunday, and for em- ployers who require their workmen to break into this time of leisure there would be a fine with a minimum of 201 r. The project, perhaps, has very little chance of passing, but that it should even be proposed, and from a quarter wlure the religious idea, as it is understood in Italy, is not very firmly rooted, is somewhat remarkable It is also a reminder of the unsatisfactory state of our own laws on the subject, which have been rendered hopelessly obsolete by the passing of time. The absurdities are so manifest that they should be I either amended or removed altogether by repeal, leaving the force of public opinion to regulate matters. For instance, horse dealing is quite a legitimate business on Sundays, but the baker must not bake bread, though he may cook his customers' Sunday dinners. Contracts may be entered into on Sunday if they are part of the regular business of the contracting parties; but apparently, while a tradesman may draw or accept a bill of exchange, such an instru- ment would be void if executed between private gentlemen only. But, of course, the most irra- tional ordinance isithat of George 111. as to con- certs and places of amusement. That charges may be made for admission if only a few seats are nominally offered to the public free, makes the whole: provision so farcical as to render a clear decision on the matter desirable in everyone's interests. Even the law in Scotland is preferable to English law on this matter, because plainer and more definite.

We have not had long to wait in Warrington for an increase in the price of bread consequent on the budget proposals of Sir Michael Hicks Beach —familiarly known as "Black Michael," a soubri- quet which will appeal to the imagination of those poor beggars to whom bread is, both figuratively and actually, the "staff of life." Last week the local Bread Sellers' Association decided to put an extra halfpenny on the price of the four-pound loaf, the impost to come in operation on Monday. We can hardly blame the ordinary retailers. They are in the hands of the bakers and millers, who seem disposed to take the opportunity of getting from the consumer rather more than Sir Michael expects from them. The new tax is 5d on 1121 b of flour, or 12Ad on 2801 b of flour, or 400113 of bread or 100 41b leaves, and consequently id on one 41b loaf. Now, if the 41b loaf be raised one halfpenny, the consumer will be paying the tax four-fold ; that is, he will be paying is 8J per cwt on flour, instead of 5d per cwt, as expressed by the Budget. When it is considered that the aver- , tage,family is,say,five persons,and the average con- sumption of bread per head of that family is at least 81b per week,it will be seen that the extra cost is 5d per week, when the Budget says it will only be 10,the 3,1 d going into the pockets of the miller and baker. It is all the inevitable result of bad and retrogressive legislation and the Government will have a lot to aniwer for when the day of reckoning comes.

In another column we publish a letter from Mr A H Crosfield which is worthy the most thought- ful perusal of all our readers. Mr Crosfield is a close student of political economy and Lational politics and his pronouncements are always based on calculated opinions. His topic now is "the war taxes" and we are sure he could not descant upon any subject possessing a deeper interest for all classes of the community than the methods by which the Government are vainly trying to extri- cate themselves from the financial muddle in which they are involved.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT. A Provincial Letter.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT. A Provincial Letter.

If the London correspondent of the "Birmingham Daily Post" has been correctly informed, and there is no reason to doubt that he has, the Provinces will alter all, be allowed to bask in the presence of , after Loudon has had Royalty,its full t o a share certain patronage e xte nt and favours at the Coronation. Anyhow, a report has reached him, lie says, to the effect that the King contemplates the possibility of paying a series of visits to certain great provincial centres immediately after the Coronation celebrations in London. No scheme, it is added, has yet been arranged, but naturally it could be no more than a small section of the more important cities that :maid receive such a visit,

which, if undertaken, would give the provinces an opportunity of witnessing a Royal progTess, which though necessarily not upon the scale of that which will be enjoyed by the Metropolis on the two great days of June 23 and 27, would serve to emphasise the unity of the country with its capital in ac- claiming the Monarch when newly crowned.

Football in every part of the country claims the majority of the months of each year From the beginning of September to the end of April,a period of eight months, it holds practically undispuLed sway. Saturday afternoon witnessed the conclu- sion of a season full of events in the provinces and the football world generally. The victory of Sheffield over Southampton, at the Crystal Palace on Saturday was,of course,a disappointment to those who had hoped a southern club would win the trophy. Yet the past Association season has shown conclusively that compared with seven or , ten years ago southern football teams have made a great advance. Unfortunately, as the "St James's Ilazette " has been pointing out, this does not : necessarily mean that the natives in the south play • more or better football, and so long as a club such as Southampton is enabled to enlist the services of , men who have not the slightest interest in the locality, and may play the next year for any other club, so lorig will Association football be deprived of the interest which a real association between the club and the players would give. On the other hand, it must be conceded that the present system provides excellent football teams for clubs that ore rich enough to hire the players. Speaking gener- ally, the very rabid football player, of whom there are not a few in both classes, Rugby and Associa- tion, does not look with delight upon the prospect of surrendering his favourite pastime, either for the joys of cricket or any other game, and if he had his way football would be cmtinued throughout the most sultry weather. This spirit, however, it is generally admitted,is displayed more largely in the , north than in the southern portions of Eugland.

Provincial readers wno have relatives and friends in Australia will be pleased to learn that within a few weeks the penny post will be extended..to that country. But the Postmaster General rias issued an official announcement which shows that the boon is not to be understood as conferred just yet. The concession is evidently intended to signalise the Coronation year of King Edward VII., and the gift is a good one.; for it will help still further to pro- mote the idea of Imperial federation. Canada, it will be remembered, established ths penny post with the Motherland at the time of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, 1897. The greater part of the financial burden incurred by the new departure will ' fall on this country ; but in Australia the letter post is twopence, so that the Commonwealth will lose considerably. But the loss will represent the concession that the Commonwealth makes to signalise the Coronation year. It is not to be at once concluded that because it will soon be possible to send a letter for a penny from Great Britain to Australia, it will he legal to reverse the process. The present indications are that the Australian co,onies will continue, except on in-coming letters, their present inland rate, and the maintenance of this rate will mean that for letters deTatched from Australia to the Mother Country the twopence- halfpenny rate will still be charged. Ths situation is no doubt anomalous, but in due time the anomaly will disappear. The ideal is, of course, the estab- lishment of a real penny Imperial post,under which it will be possible tor a penny stamp to convey a letter to any part of the forty countries embiavd within the confines of the Empire. It is worthy of note that half a century ago, this inter-linperial postal system was vigorously advocated by Elihu

One of the questions which exercised subtle in- tellects in the Middle Ages was that of how many angels could stand on the poin,-, of a needle. The savants left the question, as they did many other nice points, unsettled. But, according to " Tuber- culosis," Sir William Crooke s has come near to setting the matter at rest. For he has calculated that nine hundred tubercle bacilli can be accom- modated on the point of a small sewing-neelle,and that four hundred million bacilli can be placed on a postage stamp. All these are the seeds of 'con- sumption, and it will be easily realised what ravages on the human or animal frame 93 mighty an army commits. In the same magazine the danger is pointed out that lurks in pocke-,-handker- chiefs wed by consumptive patients It is sug- gested that cheap han 'kerchiefs should COlll9 into general use, and that these should be burnt instead of washed. "Truth" some time since advocated the use of Japanese handkerchiefs, made of soft tough paper. A Japanese lady has a roll of them in one pocket, and those she has used in another. The latter she consigns to the fire at the first oppor- tunity. Hence it is inferred that they manage some things better in Japan than we in England do.

It is not surprising to those who remember what occurred at the time of the outbreak of war between Turkey and Greece, and on other similar occasions, to find certain newspapers denouncing as " another gross imposition " an advance of one penny pr four-pound loaf of bread, as announced at Birken- head. Bakers had the temptation placed before them to take advantage of the agitation against the new duties,. and not a few have fallen before it. But there is no reason to conclude at present I that the price of bread will generally rise to any high figure during either this or the next ensuing cereal year. Bread may he regarded as cheap when it is in the vicinity of one penny per pound, and when it approaches three-halfpence, or sixpence the four-pound loaf, it is becoming dear. The Budget, however, is not the only influence that has been at work to promote the movement lately wit- nessed; because for some weeks before the Budget proposals appeared there had been a gradual rise in the markets, and the margin of profit was being approached, though it hal certainly not been reached. The flour proposal did the rest, and so bread, particularly of the inferior qualities, is in most places a fraction higher in price. than a fort- night since: But there are places in which the bakers' associations have determined to make no advance on first qualities of bread, but to enforce a " levelling up" in respect of lower qualities, with a view to suppressing ttie " cutting out" process of " cheap " bakers.

reople everywhere are naturally wondering what in a few years, will be the development of Combines and Trusts. It may give some sort of satisfaction to provincial smokers to know that as matters now stand, it is considered probable that all dis- putes between the Imperial Tobacco Company, Messrs Ogdens, limited, the wholesalers and the retailers will very soon be at an end. Not so, per- haps, the trouble between the public, the butchers and the great Beef Trust. An investigation appears to have been instituted in the United States as the result of which the kttorney-Generals department concluded that there is evidence sufficient to justify a bill of injunction restraining the Trust from pro- ceeding further under its agreement, which is regarded as "in restraint of the trade." The opera- tions of the Trust have necessarily produced an appreciable effect in this country, as evidenced in the increased price of beef in nearly all parts of the provinces. It is contended, however, by the Trust, that an advance was inevitable in any case, owing to the scarcity of bovine etoek.
E ARLEST OWN DISTRICT C FIOOL• -UNVEILING CEREMONY AND PRESENTATION,

On Saturday afternoon a pleasant reunion took dlace in the Earlestown District Schools, Rules- town, when two events of a highly interesting and imprtant character took place. The first was the utiveiling of a bust of the late Queen, and the second a presentation to Dr Handyside. There was a crowded attendance in the scheelroom,over which the Rev T R Matthews, vicar of St Jonn's, pre- sided, and amongst those present were Lord Newton, Colonel Pilkington, Canon Penrhyn, Dr Watkins, Messrs C B F Borron, Speke,J W Emmett, W Collingwood, R Stone, Dr Street, Dr Handyside, Mr A Brown (headmaster of the school) and others. A number of the children, prettily costumed, occu- pied places on the platform, which was nicely decorated. The bust was unveiled by Lord. Newton herd Newton afterwards presented Dr Handyside with a magnificent silver punch bowl, suitably inscribed.—Dr Handyside, who was much affected by the recognition of his services in such a hand- some manner, thanked them for. the magnificent gift. He said he bad no idea until a few days ago that anything of that kind was to be presented to him. 'then be only thought that it was a token of goodwill. He had no idea that his services were of such magnitude as the testimonial represented them to be. He heartily thankea the children, teachers, and good friends who had contributed to , the present. (Loud and prolonged applause.)—The Chairman said that they had not forgotten Mrs I Handyside.—Mrs Handyside was then made the recipient of a valuable silver cup and a lovely bouquet of white roses and ferns

div.head: EDUCATION BILL.
div.p: THE EDUCATION BILL.
Free Church Meeting at Runcorn.

On Tuesday evenieg at the Primitive Methodist school- room a meeting was held under tee auspices of the Free Church Council to consider the present education bill betore Parliament. Tnere was a very large attendance. Mr J Pritchard J P. occupied the chair and he was sup- ported by the Rev J Fravis(ea-president of the Primi- tive Methodist Conference), Dr W Hodson (Crewe), Revs A Wells, J Osborne, W Gay, IV A Eere, Messrs F J Norman. A R Nerman, S faylor, J Wilsoie, J Nt Frith,W Millington and others. The Chairman proposed the following resolution : This meeting of Free Churchmen protests against the Government Education Bill because (1) It violates their religious liberties • (2) It curtails their civic rights ; (3) It retards the efficiency of the education of their children ; (4) It closes a largo ma)erity of the possible appointments in the teacbiag proreesion against their children." He said that it the presect education bill were passed it would send up their modest rate ot 41 in tile £ to an enerrnour amount. There would be no auth .rity like the school Board to which they could appeal in the event of such a great expeneiture. The authorities who levied the rate would be at Chester out of control and it weuld be out of their power to obtain any redress at their hands. Clericals had always disliked 93he0l Beards and Board Schcols and be oil not doubt but it was a' their instigatien that they were new to be abo ism'. The Board of which they were jut.ty prose and the echoces which they had erected and had done such noble educatienal work were to be done away with. The Bard 0eb001.3 represented the only reveler representation of education. The bill encouraged a , multiplicity of email echo es in the interests of toe 69C. ' ! tarisne, and of which the retepayers would have to bear the burden. The object of the bill wee' to make little Anglicans. littid Romanists and even little Atheists And the Free Churchman who represented one half of the life of te.e natio were to have their consciences violatee to maintain schools with whose principles they could not agree. The Rev I Wells, seceneed. He said that ha would rather have seen his Wesleyan deitominati onal schools left out altogether r ither teen have them left in by tem,' a bill as that introduced by the present Government. It would be better for their consciences and their memories to leave to succeeding generations for the Nonconformiete of this day to baud together and fight for their principles. The Rev J Travis said that the voluntary echools were not voluntary schools save in name. Wiey should not popular education be universal ? Seine pesple thought that strong arms and weak heads were desirable. Bat Free Churchmen demanded that there should be a national system of education thorough and efficient similar to that which was obtainable in the most at- vauced of their national rivals. The present Bill dis- appointed such aspirations. It would secure the sur- vival not of the fittest but the unfittest It aimed at saving the steeple rather than educating the people. It was sectarianism against the nation. I, was the cause of the priest against the cause of the peonle. Mr Balfour himself had admitted teat N sic- coeformists had grievencee. It was not fair the' parents should send their children to schools where religion was taught with which they disagreed. Where public money was given there should be public ceuted. Now the Bill before the house would make the cage of the Nonconformists worse in many respects than i• ever was to day. It invelvei the destruction of Seheo' Boards,the endowment of sectarianism the lose of pubic representation, and the accentuation ef the religious diffieulty. He strongly condemned the bill. Dr Hodson referred to Sir John Gerst's speech the other day and criticised it in iletail. He quite aged that the Voluntary schools should be levelled up. Why should they so !mg have encumbered the ground,destror ing what they were supposed to create. It they had not beers in the way obscuring the lighiethe light would have ehone through a better system under authorities create i ad hoc. Popular control was the democratic right of the people. The Bel created a new authority which was supreme in educational matters and which was a .eriouo menace to the liberties of the people. The education Board was dominated by churchmen who would : look after their own sectarian interest, It was net what was in the bill but what was not in the bill. I, was too meagre in detail and there was too much left for the decision of the Board of Education. The bill showed no unification or there were no less than five sets of authorities ruled by the Board of Educati *fhsepeople were robbed from top to bottom of any elective power and were robbed of the right to educate their own , children. If the local authority rc fused to constitute itself an educational authority the Board of Education could step in and by man lamas compt I them. The bill was a rnest reactionary measure. _ -
During the evening -several local gentlemen adiressed the meeting.
To TM EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER!'

Sir,—We are informed that a petition in favotir of the Education Bill now b lore the Rouse of COMMO'iii is to be submitted to tie nest meeting of the Geoorsl Par poses C.mmittee. We shall not be surprised if the information proves to be true, for people who can twin f themsi Ives to accept the Bill will not hesitate at tri.flea to get it passed into law. There is no difficult* in swallowing a gnat when a camel hss clearod the way. We have car, fully followed the progress of the Elucation question for some Um., We have read the decisions of Ecclesiastical Councils pondered the demands formulated by Aoglicitra ani Roman Catholic pries,s and prelates, studied the pro visions contained in the Bill, and the only conclusion at which we can arrive is that the measure has been intro- duced at the instigation of enclesiastics and that it i. Intended ta favour the priests rather than the people— sectarianis:n rather than education.

The Bill provides for the teaching, of sectarian dogmas in schools which the ratepayers will be eomoelled to maintain and carefully exclud,a the representatives of the ratepayers from any control over the religious teaching given, but it makes no provision wha teoer to secure improvement in education. It gives the children wither b tter teachiog nor greater opportunities for intellectual advancement. Why not b 3 honest and cal it a bill fcr destroying Sheol Boards and supporting. denominational tlacbing. Had the framers of the Bill desired to promote popular eduervion they would have produced a different measure and little or no hlstility ' would have been engendered. We regard the messure as educationally unfair, as grossly unjust, and as cert.in to lead to municipal strife and sectarian bitterness. If the promoters of the Bill•beat down, all opposition, and force the measure into law, as some of them intend to do, the victory will be dearly bought and insecurely held. The Free Courchmen, who are worthy of the name, will never tamely sabmit to be taxed for teach- ing, which they regard as superstitious and untrue. Might may triumph over right for awhile but justice must prevail in the end. The following facts are known to the members of the General Purposes Committee, and will, we have no doubt, influence their course in relation t the peticim that is to be presented. 1. The Bill is an imperial and not a local. measure. 2. The Members of the committee have not; been appointed to deal with educational matters, nor have they received a mandate from their constituents to do so. 3 It would be a grave mistake to admit sectarian controversy ire° thrir delib.rations
Should the committee be asked to 9ign a politlon in favor of the Bill we hope they will ace the unreason- ableness of the request and refuse to accede to it. CHARLES FINCH-
AzDley-3treet, WArrinnton.
The Midland _Railway:—Open;ng a new Line
for Goods Traffic.

The new Midland liailway lius between New Mills and Heaton Mersey will be opened for goods and mineral traffic on Monday next. A new depot has been provided at Cneadie Heath and one will shortly be opened at Hazel Grovel (Bramhall Moor- lane.) At these depots ample accommodation for dealing with traffic of every description has !aeon provided, including goods sheds, warehouses, cattle pens, tipping docks, stacking ground for goods and coal, Sze. For the Chester Races rm. May 6th, 7th, and Sr 11, the Great Central Railway have made extensive ex- cursion arrangements. There will be extra trains co Chester on each day from Liverpool, Seacoaolo. Birkenhead Park, and Docks, New Brighcon, Bid- ston, West Kirby, Hoylsks, Neston and Parkgate. etc.; cheap express excursions from Sheffield, Seep- send, Wadsley Bridge, Ponistone, Mexboro, Swincon,Kiinhuret,Rotherham nod Masboro,Tinsiey, Broughton Lane, and Atterchtto. WIDNES DROWNING CASEC.

At the Bradley Hotel, Wiines, on Wednesday, Mr S Brighouse, county coronsr,held an inquiry touch- ing the death of an old man aged seventy years, named William Young, living at 66, Birchfield-roal, Widnes. It appeared that deceased left home early on Saturday morning with the expressed intention of going to get a truck, in Which to carry wa•hing from Farnworth Station. He did not return, and on Monday his dead body was found in a pit of water 400 yards from his home. Deceased had suffered trom pains in the side and neuralgia, and had also said he would go to the workhouse. A verdict of Found drowned" was returned. DEATH OF A. RUNCORN CAPTAIN.

At the ripe old age of 80 Captain John Abram, a familiar figure, passed away on Saturday. For some time deceased had been breaking up but the end came Somewhat unexpectedly. He had received constant and unremitting care from Dr McDougall. Deceased was engaged in the coasting trade up to attaining his fortieth year, and he was joint owner of some of the vessels of which he had the Control. Retiring from his seafaring life, he kept the Old Bridgewater Arms for a short time, and then went into his private life to enjoy the fruits of his industry and perseverance. He resided at Btanley Villv, Higher Runcorn, and was held in high esteem by a largo circle of friends. His wife pre- deceased him some six years ago. The interment took place on Tuesday at Runcorn Cemetery.
RUNCORN SO-NS OF TRIIPBRANCE.

A meeting of this society was held on Saturday night, in the Greenway-toad school, under the presi- dency of Mr Taemas Clarke. After the usual busi- ness had been disposed of, the Chairman read a paper on " Smoking," which he described as one of the great evils of the day. Some of the results of smoking were very serious. He -held that for a man to be perfectly healthy he must give up tobacco. He dealt with the argument that it was the abuse of tobacco that was wrong, and pointed out that it was a question of degree. He urged teat the practice to any extent was harmful. Men were often slaves to the vile habit. After Mr Clarke had read his paper, there was a discussion in which the following took part : Messrs Thomas Cooke, Thomas Heesom, Thomas 11 Whyte, D Bisbrown James Johnson, and Thomai J Holt.—lt was deci- ded to adjourn the discussion until the next meet- ing.

div.head: RUNCORN NO TES.
div.p: RUNCORN NO TES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.'

Judging from the town's meeting held the other day and the Council meeting on Thursday there appears every:likelihood that Runcorn will celebrate 11 the coronation festivities in a manner that should amply satisfy the most punctilious loyalist._ The proceedings will last two days, so that both adults and juveniles.will be well able to enjoy themselves to their utmost extent. The exact details are not, of coarse, yet known,for the committee appointed to consider the celebrations, have not met. It is certain, however, that the days will live lair?, in the annals of Runcorn history, for friends and foes, Churchman and Nonconformist, Conservative and ,Socialist are apparently vieing with each other to display their loyalty.

One pleasing feature already known about the proceedings is the proposition to establish the Cottage Hospital as a permanent memorial of the Coronation and the Jubilee of the Council. Mr Taylor again showed his sympathy with Runcorn interests by off ,ring towards the fund another gift of £lOO. He furthermore promised to present every Sunday and day school teacher and scholar with a medal at a cost of about £2oo—and then promised a large sum towards the fund to be opened towards defraying general expenses. There is no doubt that everyone will rally round this general fund. It will take more money chit the £2OO which the Council have been asked to give out of the rates to celebrate the proceedings in anything like the I proper style.

The Runcorn Free Caurchmen in conjunction with their brothers in other parts of the country are up in arms against the Education Bill. At a crowded meeting in Greenway-road where there were several prominent speakers the Bill was de- nounced in no weak, watery fashion. Those who were present were shown how their liberties ware being taaen away and how they were being bound to the chariot wheels of a Government who know about as much of true education as they did about the power of the Boars previous to the war. The evils of the Bill are potent and glaring. It bolsters up sectarianism at the expense of educa- tion. Nonconformists, who are the salt of the nation, are ruthlessly trampled under foot by Mr Balfour to please a bench of bishops who may be ornamental but are anything but useful. In a sense it serves the Nonconformis: Conscience right. It has sown the wind and is now reaping the whirlwind. The Liberal Nonconform- ists,deluded by the parrot-cry of "pro-Boer," put in a Tory Government to fight the country's battles. At the last election domestic legislation was not suffered to weigh one grain in the balance- And yet it is the education question, temperance reform, the housing problem, &c, &c,which mean everything to the workingman It is home affairs which touch the Britisher, while foreignoiffairs really affect him little or nothing. Suppose we had lost South Africa, with the excep- tion of Cape Colony as a coaling station, how much better off or worse off, directly, would the man in the street be ? Notlone whit. But the changes wrought by the fantastic: domestic measures of I this war Government will be yet so appalling that the Liberal Nonconformist will be sick to the heart for ever having supported such a Tory autocracy.

It is to be noted with satisfacLion that the money will not come from the poor rate, but from the general district rate, which principally falls on moneyed men. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS
Cricket.

The Warrington first eleven succeeded in placing a victory to their credit on Saturday when they visited Newton-le-Willows. Batting first, the Newton contin- gent were dismissed for the aggregate of 61, and on taking their turn at the wicket, the Warrington repre- sentatives knocked up a score of 76 for the loss of nine wickets before stumps were drawn. The capital bowling on the part of E Gibson and J Lynes, the new profes- sional, was the most striking feature of the Warrington elevens performance. Gibson secured 4 wickets at a cost of 22 runs, whilst Lynes was responsible for 5 wickets at a cost of 32 runs. It was certainly due to the excellent work of these players that the Newton total was confined to such a limit. As regarded the batting of the visitors P Hawtin and E A Connor acquitted themselves best, each of them rattling up 20. None of the other War. rington batsmen reached double figures, Lynes having the misfortune to be dismissed with a clean sheet. There was a fair attendance of spectators to witness ' the match, and winning the toss W H Hindley decided to bat on a wicket which if anything favoured the bowlers. W Turton and S Henderson were opposed by Lynes and E Gibson, the professional having a stiff breeze at his back. The opening batsmen exhibited every caution, the capital bowling being backed up with excellent fielding. With 13 runs on the board 1 Henderson played across at a fast one from Lynes, whilst Carson, who came next, was bowled Off his pads without adding to the score.

T Williams showed—a—tendency to hit, but after placing Lynes through the slips for four he was neatly taken by Hampson at the wicket. F Harrison speedily had his off stump knocked out of the ground by Lynes, whilst with the addition of three runs H Storer played one tamely into the hands of Silcock at mid-off, half the side being out for 22.

H B Hindley joined W Turton, who was exhibiting a sound defence, and the pair put a better complexion on the game as far as Newton were concerned. Eigh- teen runs were quickly added when the last corner was taken in the slips off Gibson. Two more wickets quickly fell, but W H Hindley hit out fearlessly, and the total was taken to 61 when a fine return by Briggs sent back Turton who had hard luck in not carrying his bat through the innings. The innings closed for 61.

Warrington commenced their task with P 8 Hawtin and B Silcock, the bowling being shared by C W Hindley and T Cooke. Both bowlers kept an excellent length and runs were only obtained, with difficulty. Eventually Hawtin drove Cooke finely for four and after wards turned his attention to Hindley, placing him to the leg boundary.

The score rose steadily, but at 29 Flawtin was bowled. for an excellent innings of 20. J Callon came next and imparted much vigour into his strokes. At 36 a double disaster befel the visitors, for Silcock was caught at cover whilst a good ball broke through Callon's defence A run later Lynes was taken in the slips, J W Bibby joined E A Connor, and resplute hitting by the last named placed Warrington in an advantageous position, and the issue was practically never in doubt.

The bowlers crossed over, but Connor scored freely. As 56 the Warrington captain was bowled by Cooke, and Briggs came in. After the new comer had had a narrow escape of being bowled by the first ball, Connor hit Hindley for a four and a couple, and won the match for his side. At 62, however, he was taken at the wicket Cooke bowled with success in the concluding stages of the game, and when the wickets were drawn Warrington had lost nine wickets for 76, W H Podmore taking out his bat for seven.

div.head: Cycling.
div.p: Cycling.

Saturday was beautifully fine but there was again an unusually strong east wind. The members of the War- rington club held their annual inter-Club run with the Manchester Wheelers. The destination this year was Hoo Green, that place being selected in order that a friendly match of bowls could be played on the fine large bowling green there. The Warringtonians num- bered over 20, and were met at Ho o Green by about the same number of the Wheelers. After the usual courtesies and pleasantries on both sides, the bowling match was proceeded with. Some very.exciting, games ensued, but the Wheelers were hardly in such good form as the Warrington Cycling Club members, and had to acknowledge defeat to the extent of eleven points. After the match, the combined clubs sat down to an excellent tea, provided by Mr Power, of "The Kilton," and with appetites whetted by the afternoon's sport the cyclists did ample justice to the spread. After an hour or so's pleasant chat and social inter- course, the parties separated, the Wheelers to face the gale to Manchester, and the Warrington Cycling Club to gaily free wheel all the way home, with the favour- ing breeze, after a most enjoyable afternoon's outing The scores in the bowling match were as follows :

A fine of 18s was imposed upon a Crewe workman on Monday for committing a dastardly assault upon a young lady cyclist, Miss Ethel Annie Forester,of Brown- street, Crewe. Prosecutrix stated that on Saturday night she was returning from Wrenbury on her bicycle, and when near Berkeley Towers prisoner deliberately walked in front, upset her bicycle, threw her off and injured her knee and wrist. Prisoner, who holds a bad record, said it was an accident.

A dozen cyclists had a decidedly unpleasant experi- ence in Walton road, Liverpool, on Sunday afternoon. It appears that they were riding along the road towards town.one behind the other, when the foremost rider suddenly slowed down with the result that his com- panions, being unable to pull up quickly enough, were thrown violently from their machines. The cyclists were assisted up, some bleeding freely from cuts and bruises, whilst many had their clothes torn. Several of the machines were damaged.

The very high wind which prevailed on Sunday was accountable for a singular motor-car accident at Streatham near London. A branch of a tree was blown down, and struck the driver of a motor-car, which was travelling along the high road, a heavy blow on the forehead. He I was so stunned that he lost control of the steering gear, and the motor dashed up the path and smashed into a , blank wall with such force that the driver and the three other occupants, two of whom were ladies, were thrown out of the vehicle. The ladies' injuries were of a serious character, one of them sustaining a dislocated shoulder ' and concussion of the brain, and the other a fractured skull. The driver had a leg broken. The other occupant a lad,escaped with a shaking. The motorcar was much damaged.

Mr Thomas Lee, a wine merchant's assistant, was free-wheeling down a hill at Monkton, near Ramsgate on Sanday, and the sudden application of the brake to avert a ccllision with a waggonette caused his machine to swerve, with the result that he was thrown into the road, sustaining a fractured skull. Death took place on Sunday.

In connection with the fund which the police are railing for the purpose of ob:aining a -Horse Ambu- lance for presentation to the town, a football match between the Police and Tradesmen of Earlestown was played on the ground of the Earlestown foot- ball club on Tuesday night. There wite a big crowd present, and the match was most enjoyable to the spectators, the tradesmen juet winning by a goal. Alter the match the players and others were enter- tained to a potato pie supper by Mr T Siddelev at the Railway Hotel, about 50 being present, includ- ing Superintendent Cocker of Leigh. A sociable evening was spent, Superintendent Cocker stating that it was the intention of the Police, after pro- viding the Ambulance, to help the Cottage Hospital project, a statement which was heartily cheered.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT HAYDOCK. John Heerson. a checkweigh man at the Pewsall Haydock, made an attempt to commit suicide on Wednesday. Hewson lived at 3, Carr Mill-road, Billing, and was over seventy years of age. He went to work on Wednesday. He wrote R note, leaving it on his desk. saying " You will find my body across the way." He then left his office and walked to the colliery reservoir and jumped in,but was quickly followed and pulled out. The police took him in charge,and ne was removed home and attended by Dr Mather. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, EARLES- TOWN.

The annual special service; in connection with the anniversary of the above !.unday school were , held on Sunday under favourable circtimstances. The preacher at the morning and evening services wai the Rev Robert Hind of York,and hie discourses were delivered to large congreg4tions. At the morning services the choir sang the anthem " King of Kings," and in the evening " Reliance.' In the afternoon the sacred cantata "The City of God" , was given in excellent style by the choir and chil- dren. The principal s-doists were Messrs G Ed-, monds, A Banton, Misses Mary Banton, Stronach and Woods. Mr Banton conducted. Miss Toombs presided at the piano, and Mr T A LimJnd at the organ. The colections throughout the day amounted to £62. which is a record in the annals of the Primitive Methodist Chapel at Earlestown.

div.p: MARCONI'S CAUI lON.

" Even after he had recently been so amaziegly suceessful, Marconi hesitated tetmake his achievement public, lest it seem too extraordinare for belief. Finally attar withholding the great news for two slays, certainly an evidence of sell-restraiut, he gave out a etatement te the press, and on Sunday morning tkm world knew and doubted •, on Monday it knew more and believed. Many, like Mr Edison, *welted the invest-,r'e sigaei aanouncement t afore they would credit the news. Sir Cavendish Boyle, the Governor of Newtown land, re- ported at once to King Edward ; and tie cable company which has exclusive right in Newfoundland, alarmed at , en achievement which threatened the very existence of its business, demanded that he desist from further experiments within its territory, truly an evidence of the belief of practical men in the future commercial importance of the invention. It is not a little signifi- cant of the increased willingnees of the world, beim of expanding knowledge, to accept a new sci.entifie wonder, that Mr alsrmni'e announcement should have been so eagerly and so generally believed, and Chet the plotter imagination should have leNan so fired with its poseibili- ties. One cannot bat recall the struggle against doubt, prejudice, and di belief in which the promoters of the riit trans-atlantic cable were forced to engage. Even after the first cable was laid (in 1858) and messaees had actually been trenemitted, there . Sr.' many who denied that it had ever been successfully operated, and would hardly be convinced even by the affadavits of those con- cerned in the work. But in the years since then, Eiison,Bell, Röntgen, and many other famous inventors and scientists have taught the world to be chary of Ira disbelief. Outside of this general disposi- tion to friendliness, however, Marcoal on bit own part had well earned the credit of the careful arid conserva- tive sciereist ; his previous successes made it the more easy to credit his new achievement. Fir, as an English- man (Mr Food Page), in defending Mr Marconi's announcement, has pointed out, the inventor has never made any statement in public un•il he has been abso- lutely metain of the fact; be has never had to withdraw any statemeet that he has made as to hia progress in the past. And these facts uncinestinably carried great weight in convincing Mr Bilson Mr Grattan Bell, and alien of equal note of the lit?ral truth of his Tenor'. It was astonishing how overwt7 elcningly credit came Irene every quarter of the world, ir )ne high and low alike, fnin inventors, ecientists, statessam, royalty.. Before Marconi left St John's In was already in receipt of a large mail—the inevitable letters of those who would offer congratulation, give advice, or ask favours He received offers to lecture, to write articles, to visit this, ' that, and the other place—and all within a week after , the news of Ws success. The peoole of the " ancient ' colony" of Newfoundland, famed Ifer their hospitality, crowned him with every honour in their power. I ac-ompanied Mr Marconi across !hi island on his way to Neva Scotia, and it seemed as if every fisher and farmer in that wild country had heard of him, for when the train stopped they came crowding to look in at the window."—From a highly intereving article by Ray S Palter in the May " Windsor Magazine," which is, as usual, full of good Valises, besides the first authoritative account,from the inventor' own lips, of Marconi's recent successes. Cutcliffe Hyne contrf- butes another racy record of the triumphant Thompson, and humour is well to the fore in stori•a by Spencer Leigh Hughes and Horace Bleackley—the latter pro- it ding an item which no cricketer should miss.

THE THOMAS MORRIS MEMORIAL SHIELDS.

div.head: Presentation to Heathside School Children.
div.p: Presentation to Heathside School Children.

An interesting ceremony took place at the Warrington Gymnasium on Monday evening, when the Thomas , Morris Memorial Shields were presented to boys and girls teams representing Heathside Schools. by Coun- cillor Tinnion, the Chairman of the Committee. It will he remembered that the shields were purchased by the Gymnasium Committee to perpetuate the memory of the let Mr Thomas Morris,and were offered for competition , among the scholarelattending elementary schools in the to wrasoUnfortunately the matter has not been taken up with spirit this year, the scholars at Heathside being the only entrants for the competi ion. Consequently the shields well he retained by this school for the ensuing twelve months, without a contest. Opportunity was also taken on Monday evening of presenting the medals gained by the Warrington " oh impion eight," and also those won in a recent competition for boys. Councillor TINISION presided and said that, ea chairman of the Gymnasium Committee, he was exceedingly pleased to see such a large audience, composed principally of children. The other part of the aulience consisted of the parents of the children who came to that institution to receive instruction. It was an especial pleasure to see so many mothers,as he knew the great interest they took in the education of choir children. The committee of the in i statui.on very much regretted that they were not abl to give the audience a competition instead of a display, but it was not their fault,but the fault of the managers and masters of the various day schools of Warrington,who evidently did not think it ot sufficient importance to compete for the Morris Shields, which bad been provided by tlde.com- mittee of the Gymnasium. The shields had been pro- vid3d to perpetuate the memory of the late Mr Thomas Morris, and he was sorry that that matter had net received greater attention from the managers and masters of the schools to whom he had just alluded. The only competitors this year w,-re boys and girls con- nected with Heath Side schools—(applause)—who had had a clear" walk over," and wou!ci retain the shields for the neat twelve months. HQ ha t great pleasure in presenting the shields, on behalf of the schools he had named, to the headmaster, Mr Parker, and on behalf of the committee he thanked him and his school managers for their appreciation of the work of the Gymnasium Committee, which was part and parcel of the instruction that should be given to children. (Applause) lie was pleased to see that the Education Department were waking up to the fact that drill and instruction were a necessary part of the education of a child. It was important to have chi'dren educated in reading, writing, and arichmetic.—training for the mind—but it was also important that their bodies should be trained to give them health. He hoped that another year trey would have a kohl competition tor the !Miele& (Applause) The speaker having paid a ! c ,nspliment to the skill of the gymnastic instructor, Mr Kinsley, presented the shields to Mr Parker. _ _

Mr PARKER stepped forward, amid applause, and said it wou'd nave been a grsater pleasure to have had a competition for the shields. He hoped that next year other schools would enter. Ho 'would sooner lose in a good competition than win without nropstition. (Hear, hear, and applause ) Master REGGIE TINNION, the five year old son of the Chairman. then presented the medals to the champion 8 as follows :-1, prize champion (special gold medal), C , Sinclair ; 2, A Parr ;3, A Ashton ; 4, C Roher's ; 5, G E Hayes ; 6, a a,1,-,ocay ; 7, J Ge dors, and 8, 0 Corbett. Miss Afar TnarioN, 'hi Chairman's daughter, then presented the four medals woa in the comp, tido-) for the boys as follows 0 Sinclair ; 2, S Green ; 3, E Bowen ; and 4, H . .

During the evening; an exceilent gymosatie display was given with dumb-bed 4, rin;s, bar bells„parallel and harizmtal bars,and single stieki,the tug of war between tolys and girls creating considerable interest. The girls amid a scene of excitemeot gained the victory.

div.head: MOSQUITOES WORSE THAN BULLETS.
div.p: MOSQUITOES WORSE THAN BULLETS.

Prohahly not more than Gne in a thouiand of us has witnessed a battle, oar conoeptione cf those terrible evento being geuerally derived from verbal and pictor- ial description. Fr the most part, impressions so nle- tained are utterly erroneous. The spectacle of two hostile forces appreaching closely to each other, with flags tieing and banners waving te the accompaniment of music, with which so many great painters have made us familiar, has not occurred within the memory of man. Fu. the oerehatante to come to dole quarters is extremely rare, and certainly never happen.; on a large !male. Once we witness] a sharp fight between Americans and Spaniards ; but it made a poor show. IV Span'ard_. could be seen at all. theueh now and again an American would fall wounded afrer a sputter of fire which appeared to come out of a clus,er of trees half a mile away. Nevertheilvis the Spaniards were beaten and made off, and the Americans returned to their tents saying many hard :hinge of the Cuban mosquitoes, which they dreaded vastly more than the bullets of the enemy. The most interesting of all battles take place within ourselves. When one feels unwell and is disinclined to effort, but forces himself te the desired action, that is a battle—in inevitatle battle, for in such circumstances you muit conquer or be conquered. Your cannot cry off, because you carry your enemy about with you. Victery can n ly be assured by employing the best weanon, as Mrs F Chapman, of Lonebedge, Coriley,near Warminster, did. .• Thre rears ago," raid Mrs Chap- man. on 22nd January, 1902, " I had Some severe attacks of indigestion. Immediately after eating, my heart aced to Palpitate, followed by the inevitable pain in the chest, which sometimes penetrated to the back. I dared not eat solids— not so much even as an ego—but Herd on iiquid fool. On tieing in the morning, I was generally tired and de- pressed,and my tongee thickly coated. All these troubles my doctor attributed to impaired digestion. As I con- tinued to grow worse, I begin to fear there was no cure for me, when one day a little hook arrived by post des- cribing cavil effected by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. After reading and discussing it with my husband, he persuaded me to try it., which, happily, I did. I took in all only four bottles of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup and, hopeless as my case bad seemed, soy rncovery wag rapid and complete. I have not takea a dose of the Syrup for a long time now, not having needed it, hut all the same I like to have a bottle of it in the house."

An accident occurred in Knutsford-road on Mon- day On the approach of a tram a horse attached to a cab became very restive, and unfortunately it backed the cab to whirl it waq attached into the tram. The result was that the cab was turned over and damaged, but there was no other serious result.

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
Final Tie.
Warrington Secure the 1 rophy.

Though the season is at its fag-end there was a great amount of interest manifested in the final tie for the South-Wet Lancashire Cup on Tuesday evening, when Warrington and Widnes met to decide whioli club should be the holder for the next twelvemonths. The Runcorn ground was the one se!ected for the occasion,being easily accessible to the supporters of the contest- ing clubs, and the evening being beautifully fine, one of the largest crowds seen at Runcorn for some time assembled. A good thousand came from War- rington, while nearly as cany crossed the river from Widnes. •Altegether there would be about 5.000 present at 6.30, the time fixed for the kick-off The ground it-ielf was in fair order,thougifdistinctly hard owing to the dry spell of weather. In the estimation of the spectators Warrington were favourites at the outset, and were expected to prove their superiority on this, the third time of meeting the Widnesians this season. The two pre- vious engagements had resulted in a win for Widnes by 2 goals to a try on their own groand,and a drawn game at Warrington when there was no score. Warrington looked to be easy winners of the cup on points, but rather lucky victories ever Runcorn and Leigh brought Widnes up to the same level, .and Tuesday's deciding match was thus necessitated. In the South West Lancashire Com- petition the records of the two teams are as follow : Points

P. W. L. D. F.)r ag;t. Pte. Warrington 10 ... 7 2 ... 1 ... 74 ... 42 ... 15 Widne Both clubs were well represented in the final tie, Warrington turning out as selected, and playing their strongest fifteen with the exception of the injured caprain D I.herwood. Widnes were with- out Peacick, his place being taken by Cullen. The players and officials were as follows ; Widnes : Kinsella, full beck; Hughes, Tilley, Rispan. Cullen, three-quarters; Douglas and Lally, half-backs; Aspey, Harop.on, Lynch, Riley, Curtis, Webster, Ai Donald and Ken3.on, forwards. Warrington : Hallam, full-back; Fish, Hocken- hall, Dickenson and Harris thresquarters; Allen and Burgess halfbacks ;Board m an, Niorrison. Bdrnondson, Eden, J Swift, W Swift, Roberts and Forster, for- warde.

Referee: Mr B &Osten Werneth). Touch judges : Messrs J H Houghton (St Helens) and J Ellison (Runcorn). Warrington won the toss, and elected to play with a cross wind slightly in their favour. Widnes started and Roberts responded powerfully after a mark. Warrington soon rushed down, but Burgess was upset, and Widnes dribbled to the centre. Hallam was here thrown in touch by Hughes. A stoppage wae caused a moment later through Eden sustaining a na4y crack on the knee. Dickenson punted powerfully, but Aspey marked and play ruled even. Douglas get hold from the pack but was up.et by Allen. Lally wes penalised for pre- mature werk,and Fish nearly landed a goal.llughes deliberately knocked on in front of the posts. and Fish tried again, the ball passing just outside. Hesitation by Hallam let Warrington down, Widnes reaching the quarter flag, where Hughes fouled Fish. Lynch next had an abortive shot at goal. Then Foster earned cheers by a dashing run into Widnes territory. Widnes did a lot of lofty kicking, and the Warrington backs were none too steady. Fish received from Hocken- hall and inaugurated a hot attack on the Widnee line. Morrison made a great effort but was held outside. Again Lay ran offside and Hallam failed at a penalty. Rigby marked and Dickenson mulled the return badly. Exciting Work followed but play settled down again at centre, Kinsella getting badly shaken in echerge. A kick by Lally led to Widnes getting near the Warrington line, Hughes being pulled down by Dickenson. W Swift got his head badly cut and was assisted off. Rispan dropped at goal and missed. Widnes rushed des. perately and Hallam saved grandly on the line. Tho next mince Lally dropped a goal from the rear of the pack. Whines had the best of matters, Lally trying to repeat his previous performance but fail- jog badly. Fish at last ran down and centred, Cullen clearing in the nick of time. Warrington attacked again and got a penalty in good posi- tion, • Fish equalising amidst great cheer- ing. Widnes came back with a big rush Burgess mulling close in. Rispan dropped again and missed, Warrington immediately racing to the other end where Fish marked prettily and landed another goal, the uproar being tremendous. War- rington's bad fielding was often dangerous and just on the interval Hockenhall would have let Widnes in but he fortunately knocked on. Half time, War- rington two goals, Widnes one goal. Roberts restarted and Aspey soon made the usual mark, Dickenson once again mulling the catch. Widnes attacked, Hughes nearly getting in from Tilley's pass. Then Burgess got away finely in his own quarter and after brilliant passing by Dicken- son and Hockenhall, Fish ran in behind the posts, The scorer took the goal kick but just missed. Great efforts were now put forth by both sides, Widnes attacking and getting a penalty near the line. Tilley took the kick, but filled. A lot of exchange kicking followed and then a sen- sational incident occurred,Forster being sent off for tripping Kinsella. Warrington now had a hard time of it with only six forwards, but a penalty kick came in nicely at a critical moment. Then a fine punt and run by Dickenson carried play to centre again. A pass by Douglas to Tilley resulted in another drop which was unsuccessful. Once more Dickenson was erratic and fielded shockingly. Wid- nes passed, Cullen being grassed by Harris. The Widnes forwards made a strong rush but Hallam took the hall from them and dribbled clear. War- rington still had to play a defensive game and did so very soundly,. though the Widnes attack cvas not very scientific. For once in a way Warrington changed the venue. Eden charging down Tilley's kick. Play was soon beck to the leaders' quarter, however, Hallam marking grandly near the goal. Then Hughes ran round and passed across to Cullen who was only stopped at the corner by Harris. Aspey tried a tricky penalty along the floor close in, hut Harris got the ball first. the War- rington partiz ins cheering vociferously. From new to the close Warrington gave Widnes an example of marking which even Aspey must have admired.

The end came with a mighty cheer for the victors Warrington 2 goals 1 try, (7 points); Ft idnes 1 goal (2 points). COMMENTS.

The cup was fairly won by the better team, and it is a feather in Warrington's cap to have kept their line intact though finishing the game with two men short, and three others almost totally crippled for the time being Roberts, Boardman and Eden were all lame, so that there were only three sound forwards left when Swift retired and Forster received roarchieg orders. Still Warring- ton showed smarter football all through than Widnes, who are not, as 1 have remarked before, quite in the same class as the Warringtontans. Forward they are superior both in scrimmage work and dash in the leo,e, but behind t,hey lack the speed and combination of he senior leaguers. The game was by no means a poor one for a cup final and the interest never flagged from start to finish. Both teams were trying desperately hard, and when Warrington were fully repre- sented there was a probability of their scoring any time. The loss oi Swift made a big difference, and Lally took the opportunity of dropping a goal. For a few minutes Warrington looked like a defeated team under the double mis- fortune, but Fish lead the way to the other end and within ten minutes he had made the scores equal. [ Five minutes later and Warrington were ahead, the: same player landing a second clever goal. Though Warrington lost a second forward after half-time, the game was won when Fish put the finishing touch on a round of passing by scoring a try near :the posts. The effort was a brilliant one from its [ inception by the clever Warrington half, Burgess, Ito the point of its culmination, and showed the Warrington backs at their best. Defensive play was the order after this, and in view of Warring- ton's weakened forces it was the correct game. Marks were made with automatic regularity and even A4spey, the champion of markists, smiled a sad sweet smile. Individually, Burgess, Fish and Hallam were the best men on the winning side, all three playing sound. clever football. Allen hnd Harris came next, but Dickenson we., t erratic to merit praise. Morrison was the beet of the forwards, who all worked hard, and especially so when short-handed. On the Widnes side Kinsella played very well in the rear, while Lally was tbe best man on the attack, the threequarters being outclassed and also showing a fatal predilection to drop at goal instead of go for the line. The for wards were all excellent, and were ably led by Aspey, who though net a popular man, is a clever footballer. " WETTING" THE CUP.

Immediately the whistle sounded there were mighty cheers for the winners, and then a wild rush by the crowd across the ground, in the direc- tion of the stand, in front of which the cup shone in all its glory Fish was almost carried from the enclosure, and when he appeared a moment later in the centre of the stand with the cup in his possession the cheering was renewed Mr Houghton made the presentation in 3 few euitable words, at the same time handing the Warrington sub-captain the handsome gold medal he had won. Then followed popping of corks and the c nitentis of three bottles of champagne were poured into the cup, to which each member of the team placed his lips in a long and loving caress. Isherwood was present and as captain of the team he of course cams in for a lick at the pot. These proceedings did not last long, and the players and supporters departed for Warrington,where a cordial reception awaited them.

div.head: AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AT WARRINGTON.

A huge crowd and a couple of bands awaited the artival of the cup-holders, who made a procession through the principal streets of the town on board a 'bus, with the cup prominently displayed in front. There was a lot, of cheering and jubilation, especially when the Bridge Inn was finally reached. It is so long since the Rugby team brought a cup home that the popu- lace was delighted with the novelty and the success was immensely gratifying. It has been no easy capture and for the second time Warrington have fairly and squarely won the South-West Lancashire cup. That they may place others alongside it in days to come is the hearty wish of " OVALIST."

div.head: NORTHERN UNION CUP. The Final Tie. Broughton Rangers v. Salford,
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION CUP. The Final Tie. Broughton Rangers v. Salford,
Brilliant Victory of the Rangers.

The Most important club event in the Northern Rugby Union season, the final tie of the Cup Competition, was decided on Saturday afternoon at Rochdale. the contesting teams being Broughton Rangers and Salford. The fine per- formances of both teams in the competition, and the feet that they bed finished at the bead of the Northern League table, combined to make the struggle more than usually interesting. The arrangements carried out by the Hornets' officials on the well-appointed Athletic Grounds were admir- able. It was wisely decided to close the cheap stand rather than run the slightest risk of accident, but the accommoda- tion without it was quite equal to the demand, not more than 16,009 people being present balford were late In arriving and it was nearly four o'clock before a start was made Broughton played Willie James at half back, to the exclusion of Barrett, and 0 Thompson deputised Ruddick in the:forwards Salford turned out just as *elected. The afternoon was fine.but there was a very strong' wind Flowing towards the town goal, and Wileon,tho Rangers capteln, had the good fortune to win the toss. In th first ten minutes little advantage was gained from the use of the wind, the work of the Salford men during that period 'being exceedingly fine. They came very near scoring once. Widdeson not far from his own line missed fielding, and Tom Williams was seen at the head of a dangerous-looking rush, but the ball rolled into touch before he could reach it, Widdesen atoned for his mistake en the kick out by following up aad tactkliag Smith finely before he could dispose of the ball. For a time play was mainly in the Rangers' quarters. The forwards appeared to he working hard on both tides but the Salford men behind were smarter on the ball, and tackled with grim earnestness. In time the Rangers fouad their bearings, and aided by the wind, changed the venue to the Salford half. Wilson at once began to make things lively for the defenders. Willie Jamse had a shot at goal from a penalty, and showed wonderful judgment in allowing for the wind, but I he ball dropped short. The Bangers' backs ehewad seine pretty combination. but fora time they were kept in check. Salford got to the ether *nil as the result of Harry's naistield- in pan. and the Rangers turned but bthiet wtaableosnliTaaa mostisnentshaetional manner. From a stiff scrummage in their own half the Broughton forwards get possession. Sam James burst away from the pack, and though nearly tackled, managed to pass out to Marry. The latter took the ball splendidly, and transferra I to Wilson, who, taking the ball on the run, went at a great speed towards the Salford line. Hogg backed him up, but the Rangers' captain tricked Smith and scored a magnificent try behind the posts Willie James easily kleeed a goal. This was the commeneement of a long and fruit- ful attack on the Salford line. Soon after the drop-out James almost scored, and Wilson was only just pulled down a foot or two short of the crease. Hogg. too, experi- enced hard lines in not crossing at the corner. trice relieved the position with a clever run, and the Salford forwards strove hard to make amends, but there was further trouble in store for the Reds. The batiks on the Salford side et srted a Passing movement, which ended in disaster—to themselves. Intercepting Williams' transfer to his centre partner. Bab Wilson agile got clear, and gave this time to Hogg. Smith could not cope with the movement, and the Rangers' right wing three-quarter heel a gratuitous passage over, Despite this double reverse, the Salford team played up pluckily. Half-a-dozen chances came their way in as many minutes to rub off some of the adverse balance, but it mutt he admitted that the efforts of the back division at critical moments were painfully weak. The Salford men, incl word, could do nothing right, and te complete their discomfiture the übiquitoue Wilson put the closure on their lake-warm efforts by registering another sensational try. As on the last occasion he snatehed an opportunity of taking an opoonenYe pass In the Brought°a quarter, and darted off up the touch line side. Ho passed to Hogg near the centre, but the latter did not field the boll properly. Wilson was close to him, and raking in he ball again before it touched the ground the Broughton skipper do iged Smith in simple fashion, and cantered over the line with his second try, from which V, James scored as easy goal. This brought the interval, the score giving Broughton a clear lead of 15 points—three goals and three tries to nil. The exhibition in the second half, except in the con- cluding stages, would not bear comparison with the pre- Interval play. The listigera played five threequarters,White- lead being brought out of the pack. Salford started well, same goad work by the forwards being followed by a brave dash the byho was pulled down in close proximity Williams,to Wliniell."mbasM James was esbviously suffering from a damaged shoulder, but the defense of his eolleagues was eleven Salford missed some glorious opportunitiee he the first half-hour with the wind at their backs. Once Griffiths put in a long kieg, and Price tackled Fielding, leaving the ball completely at the wirer if Bone, who failed to utilise the fistest opportunity of the match. A passing movement by Wilson and Hogg ended in the latter being brought down a yard from the Salford line, As a set-off to this, Bone got peesession in the Salford quarters, and with no one but the full back to beat made a sensational run. Widdeson, however, went after him, and cleverly hauled him down from behini. For a good portion of the time, however, the play was scrappy and scrambling in the extreme, and come exhibitions of bad temper did nut tend

Near the close Wilson wound up a sucerb afeernoon's work by scoring another glorious try, which was cleverly converted by Orem, bat eveu this eff .rt was eclipsed by Widdeson who, getting a pass from Sam James, ran round his opponents in brilliant fashion and put the seal on the Rangers' success by notch- ing the fifth tr.,. div.head: NORTHERN RUGBY LEAGUE. --- Formation of a Second Division.
div.p: NORTHERN RUGBY LEAGUE. --- Formation of a Second Division.

A joint meeting of the Northern Rugby League and the Yorkshire Senior Competition was held al Huddersfield on Monday night, lalr A Clifford, Huddersfield, presiding, the meeting being practically an adjournment from Friday,April la. The Northern League states that since their last meeting they had held confeseeces with the Lancashire Senior Com- petition, and that body pointed out that if the present York- shire Senior Competition and Lancashire Senior Competition were to be carried on. with a deaiding match for promotion between the two, it would leave them with au insufficient number of class clubs to carry out a satisfacto:y programme The Lancashire Senior Compe. ition asked the Northern League to assist them in forming a streng second division of the League, and this the Northern League had promised to do The propdsal of the League was to torm two divisions of 18 clubs each, yell divisions to be formed thus :—Take the fourteen clubs in the Northern League, the first eight clubs In the Yorkshire Senior Competition. and the first eight in the Lancashire nenior Competition, making in all thirty Mobs. Let such thirty clubs v.ite the four vacancies for the First League which would leave the clubs eighteen in the first division and twelve in the second division. Then invite the clubs remaining tom the Senior Competition, in addi- tion to other suitable clubs, and seleet from the applications six clubs to make the second division into eig teen clubs. The Northern League retired from the room to allow the Yorkshire Senior Competition to consider the propoeal, but before retirins stated that whatever decisioes they might arrive at on the qeestion of the seco ,d division of the League they were prepared to agee with the proposals m mdc at the I last Huddersfield meeting namely—(l) The withdrawal of the boycott ; (2) to arrange a mutual, transfer law ; (3) that players oc registers of both the Northern League and the Yorkshire senior Competition shal, belong to the club last played with, subje •t, to the payment of a transfer fee, to be fixed by an impartial commission, failing payment of such transfer fee to belong to his old °lnt). Tie Yorkshire senior Competition then cmssidered the question of proposed second division' and decided that they could not agree to join such second division, as, in their opinion, it would not be to the best interests of the Yorks Lire Senior Competition clubs. An agreement was finally arranged between the Northern League and the Yorkshire Senior ilompetition on points 1,2, and 3 The Noithern League accepted the deci- sion of the Yorkshire Senior Competition with respect to the promoted second division. Messrs Waller and Burnley, pre- sidents of the Northern Union, and Rich, hon. secretary of the Cumberland County Union. were ag, eed upon as the commissioners. It was understood that notwithstanding the decision of the Yorkshire Senior Competition with res- pect to the secous division of the League such second divi- sion will be formed, and admission to tie first division will be only through the second division.
