The enlargement of Christ „Church,

div.head: Latchford.
div.p: Latchford.

An interesting event in the history of Christ Church, Latchford, took place on Saturday afternoon, when Mrs George D kin performed the ceremony of laying the foundatiou stone of the extension which is to be carried out at the church in order to provide additional accommodation for worshippers. The necessity for an enlargement has long been obvious, and Messrs William and Seger Owen, architects.havine teen consulted,it has been decided te build a north aisle which will furnish accommodation for over 100 worshippers. The eaten. sion will be made by taking down the west gable to the notees transept end carrying it along to the main north wall. The old north windewe to the nave will be rebuilt In the new north wall, which is lineable with the old transept wall. As far as possible the whole of the old stone work will be utilivd. The builder is Mr Harry Fairclough, while the contrect for the stonework was let to Mr Ephraim Aukland Holiest-in-street. The colt is estimated at about £1,200, and we understand that it is intended at some future date to carry out a s one porch to the new door on the north side of the church. —There was a large congregation to witness the laying of the foundation stone. A short service was conducted by the V‘car (the Rev F A Screeton) commencing with the hymn "The Church's one foun- dstion." The choir was in attendance, and Mr Fry, the °reenlist at the church, officireed as accompanist. Psalm 122 having been sung, the laying of the stone took place. A bottle coitaining copies of the three local newspapers was put into the cavity of the stone, which bore the inscripaion " Enlarged 1902," and a handsome trowel beating the inscription " Mrs G Dakin, on the occasion of laying the foundation stone of the new north aisle, Christ Chirch, Latchford, April 26, 1902," was handed to the lady, who laid the founds ion stone in the neinl manner' making use of the following words,—" In the faith of Jesus Christ, and in the name of the Holy Trinity, we place this foundation stone, which I declare to be well and truly laid." The Vicar then delivered a short address, and said that a ceremony of that kind was lone which, after all, was not without considerable interest and meaning. It had a very deep hatorest to those who belonged to Christ Church, because it marked the beginning of a new epoch in its history. This was the second time the church had been enlar 'ad : it was, he believed ,enlarged in the year 1875, and the original building consisted of the present nave and the chanceLso that the church was going on increaaing. When St. John the Baptist spoke 31 Jesus Christ, he said, " He must increase," and their own church was dedicated, not to any saint, but Christ Himself, and they might say of the church that it was increasing. And so that extension was, he hoped, not merely a material extension, but the outward sign of the extension of the influence of the Church of Christ in the parish of Christ Church, Latchford And they were proud not merely because it was an extension of their Particular church, but that the work of the Church of England was still going on. They belonged to the old- est historical body in this country ;there was no religious body which could compare with the church of England in it antiquity, traditiens, hiseorical assoeiations and interest, and it had still a mission for the nation after 1,500 years of history. The fact that they were gathered together that day on a work of that kind , allowed that the Church of England WAS still a living bmiy,and that it had still a messa,n3 for the people. And then the foundation stone laying was a symbol of the I fact that they bed given expression to in the hymn that Christ was the one foundatioe of the Church. In con- 'elusion the rev gentleman asked the audience te pray, as he hoped they had continually prayed, that the work of Christ might go en and presper.—Mr Dikiie, on be- half of Mrs D ikin, expressed her appreciation of the great honour which bad been conferred upon her in having been asked to perform the cetemony. He ex- plained that she consented with considerable diffidence because she thought there were others/ who had a prier claim, and it was only on the assurance that eit was the unanimous wish of the committee that also consented. He thanked them all for their kind- TICSS.—The proceedines concluded with the singing of the hymn "0 Lord of hests."—A collection was made in aid of the extension fund.

div.head: WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL WARRINGTON.
div.p: WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL WARRINGTON.
The Anniversary.

This annual function took place on Sunday and ' was as successful as any of its predecessors. An effort was made to raise £5O, and this sum was a:- most realised, the collections totalling up to £45 12s 7d. Fine weather favoured the occasion in contrast to the many wet anniversary days which have been experienced in counection with Wycliffe Sunday School. The seating accommodation of the choir bad been temporarily increased in ordtr to accommodate the Sunday scoool choir at the after- noon service. There was a beautiful display of spring flowers on the communion table, daffodils and tulips predominating. The morning service was well attended and was a good augury for the rest of the day. The school children were accommodated in the gallerie's and their voices were heard to advantage in several i hymns. One hymn was sweetly sung by the infants who were led by Mr Joseph Po:it:flora. The preacher for the occasion was the tier Lincoln Jones, 8.D., A.T.S., of Roby Chapel, nano:lest er, and he based an appropriate discourse on this text " What then shall this child be ?" (Luke i. c, 60 v.). He pointed out that this was a common question because they were all aware of the momentous possibilities of child life. It was the formative period of life, and if we neglected the training of the children we must pay the penalty in producing men without manliness and women without woman- hood. The main responsibility rested upon the parents and the home either made or marred the child. The preacher proceeded to show that not only had the parents a distinct duty towards chil- dren but the church had also a duty to perform. Ile preferred to think of the Sunday School as every bit as important and essential as the work of the church

In the afternoon thlre was a large congregation at the combined meeting of Sunday scholars and members of the P.S.A. when a service or song entitled "Tae Reformation," or the life work of Martin Luther, was rendered by the scholars and choir. Mr William Brown conducted and a num. ber of carols, anrhem-,and choruses were efficiently sung. Solos were contributed by Mrs Gleave, Miss Travis, Miss Hill, Mr A Griffiths, Mr Gauld and Mr A Cotterill, and the efforts of the vocalists were greatly appreciated. Mr W El Payton, Mus Bac pre sided at the organ. Mr A. Corney gave the connec- tive readings which gave a briof biographical sketch of Martin Luther. Mr George Wallington, the superintendent of the school, made a brief appeal on behalf of the Sunday school funds. The service concluded with the singing of the hymn " Onward Christian Soldiers."

The church was well filled at the evening service when the pulpit was occupied by the Rev A Good- rich, D.D , of Chorlton-road, qanchester. He preached an able discourse on "The inward man." The four great features of the inward man, he said, were (I) personality the senz-e of " I am," (2) the s4-‘nse of duty, (3) the sense of God, (4) the sense of sin, He proceeded to show how these different features of the inward man existed in different persons in different states and degrees. In some persons, the inward man seemed dead, hut without toe life of the inward man there could be no real knowledge of God and it was only as the inward man was thoroughly alive that we had true fulness of life. In an able and characteristic man- ner the preacher proceeded to show that there was only One Who could give life to and quicken each element of the inward man and that One was Jesus Christ. The choir sang an anthem at both the morning and evening services Appropriate hymns were sung and heartily joined in by the congregation.

div.head: DEAN AND THE LOVER.
div.p: THE DEAN AND THE LOVER.

While he looked, the figure turned its bead,and lifted the candle high to see him the better. What an odd fizure it was ! It was that of a man about sixty, dressed in clerical gash of an ancient cut, with white bands, and wearing on its bead a bag-wig. Kura plumy Brandon stared. The strange person looked at him with a piercing gaze from cavernous eyes, The face was ivory-pale, and was furrowed with the track of storms. Bitterness and desolation were in its expression. "So you have awakened, sir," the visitor said grimly. " I don't know how I earns te fall asleep," answered Humphrey Brandon apologetically. " I suppose you are . . . the Dean ?" "lam the Dean," the other replied, "I must have slept some time." Humphrey Brandon looked at his watch. "By Jove, halt pest twelve ? It was only half-past six when 1 came in. How did I come to do it ? I was on my way to keep . . appointment." " With Amaryllis or with Margaret ?" Humphrey Brandon stared at the sardonic face. " How do you know ?" be began, stammering. "I am no wizard," she other replied. " You talked in your sleep. Amaryllis, Margaret ; no scale could have balanced them more evenly." The hue of guilt crept into Humphrey Brandon's face. His lashes,dark and curling Ilk, a girl's, fell on his cheeks. " You are aocox- combe," said the old man severely, putting down the candle in its old-fashioned candle stick on the librarian's desk. Some wild impulse to make confession end ask Gourmet Came over the young , man. He flung himself with a reckless air into one of I the worn leatiser-eovered (theirs. " Perhaps I am," he said humbly. "Anyhow, Mr Dean, you are ghostly,and I Need ghostly counael." The Dean snuffed the candle. with a whimsical smile en his full lips. "It is your duty to help erring mortals. Will youmot take the chair oppAite to mine, and listen to me ? " The Dean took the chair. and dropped his cheek upon his hand. The bag-wig fell either side his face. Humphrey Bras- don stared at him. Who was it he was like as he sat so ? Same bsffling memory played about the young man's mind and eluded him. He forgot it then, fascinated by the eyes in their cavernous hollows. They were burn- a3 though they needed the slaking of tears. The face was the face of one deeply unhappy. It was easier to peur out the tale of his vacillation to , such a face. When he had finished tem was a pause. I Then tke men opeotite him sighed so hollowly that the young man started. " I said you were a coxcomb!' I said the Dean, " but you are only a fool. You must ge back to Margaret. Not for all the Amaryllises in the world would yen break Margaret's tweet. And you would break it, though she might live for twenty years after it was broken and show you alw lye a smiling face. There are such women."—From " The Meeting in the Library," in the " Comilla Magazine " ler May.

The Spiritualist Bazaar. The bazaar in aid of the building fund in con- nection with the Warrington Spiritualist Society was continued on Saturday. At the opening pro- ceedings the President took the chair,and in intro- ducing Mrs Fryer, who was to declare the bazaar open, spoke of her early connection with the society, being in fact, as Miss Kate Ribchester,their first "minisior," and stated the pleasure with which the committee welcomed her that day.— Mrs Fryer recalled her first visit to the society, and stated how she had watched the progress of the cause in the town, and the pleasure it afforded her not only to see some of the first members still in harness but the new members who had been added to spread the truths of Spiritualism. She felt proud to take part in this their first bazaar, and after declaring it open trusted that the workers would meet with great success.-1 vote of thanks to Mrs Fryer was moved by Mr G Willcock, seconded by Mrs Sher- burn, and heartily carried, and after Mrs Fryer had responded the sale was proceeded with.—During the afternoon and evening a number of friends gave musical stud vocal selections, and a . humorous sketch entitled The Black Dwarf " afforded con- siderable amusement.—At night the room was crowded, several friends horn other denominations being present, and the bazaar, as a first attempt. may be considered a success.

Sunday Trams and 'Buses. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me sr ale in your paper to prote,t against the running of trams and 'buses o 3 the Sabbath Day. Ido not see that it is either necessary or justifiable to have a Sunday service of trains and 'buses, and I am extremely sorry that the management of the trams have not seen their way clear to exclude Sunday service. May I urge upon all Churches, Missions, and P.S.A.'s to pass resolutions against Sunday traffic, and forward them in the first instance to the Town Council, and in the second instance to the 'bus proprietors. May I also further suggest, sir, that the Warrington Church Union, the Warrington Free Church Council, together with their Roman Catholic friends, take apeedy steps to send deputations to the "powers that be," in order that we may have a respite of Sunday tram and 'bus services. —Yours, &C.,
ANDREW SCRIVEN.

THE FACE AT THE WINDOW.—Jnne Darwell, married woman. was summoned by Alice Platt, single woman, for assaulting her on the 22nd of April.—The evidence showed that the prosecutrix was in the habit of staring in at the defendant's window, and this was greatly resented. As prosecutor did not desist when requested defendant smacked her face three times,—Defeadant was let off with paying the costs 45 6d THE SClLOCKLlOARD.—Forneglacting to send their children to school William 13urke was fined 6d and costs, and Annie Jones the same sum. ALLEGED TECETT Q IRON—Joseph Wood, waterman was charged on romand with stealing a chain of iron value 105 belonging to Prank Hallowby. The evidence showed that the chain was left in prosecutor's boat lying near iVigg's Works. It was alleged that the prisoner stole it from the boat and afterwards sold it on the 15th to Mr Howard', marine store dealer, for 9d. Prosecutor said that the chain bad no distinguishing marks about it but he was almost certain that the chain was his. Prisoner did not deny selling the chain but contended that ke had picked the chain up off Ifastharn Beach when fisbing.—Prisoner's son corroborated the finding of the chain and the prisoner was discharge S.

div.head: Celebrations. --- Coronation Proposals at
div.p: Celebrations. --- Coronation Proposals at
Runcorn.
Generosity of Mr. Taylor.

Oa Monday evening a public meeting was convened at the Technical Institute, Runcorn, [or the purpose of considering in what form the Coronation of his Majesty King Edward VII. should be observed in the town. Mr S raylor (chahman of the Urban District Council) occupied the chair, and supporting him on the platform were—Rev Canon Wood (vicar). Rev C R Killick (vicar Holy Trinity), Rev Father Chambers, Rev J Osborne, Rev H Morrison, Rev J B Forster,Rev W A Es re, Rev W Gay, Messrs F J Norman, R H Posnett, E Imison, P R Allen, W Handley, A R Norman, E Marshall, J Willing, S C Beckett, F A Lake. and others. In the body of the hall there were—Revs %V Scholes and E S Oliver, Messrs James Pritchard, J R Frith, .1 M Frith, T A Lawrenson. W Millington. 'I Wood, W Hankinsen, W Graham, T Cooke, J Douglas, G Hewitt, D Bisbrown, S Pope, J Scraeg, W H Mack, J K Digges, E Gatley, H Turnbull, and others. There was a lerae attendance. The Chairman said he, had calied that meeting in ' order that they might discuss and decide what steps they should take to celebrate the King's Coronation. They had two days to provide for, via., the 26-h and 27th Juno, and that made the cirucmstances different to what they were on the occasion of her late Majesty's Jubilee. He happened to be chairman of the Council in 1897, and he remembered a good deal about the festivi- ties on ttat occasion. In the forenoon they had a pro- , cession of magistrates, friendly end trade iocieties, and the various public bodies ; in the afternoon a procession of school children, with subsequent festivities at their various schools. He presumed it would be their desire to proceed on somewhat eiroilar lines on the occasion of the Coronation. The pleasure and advantage of the people were the two things they had to bear in mind. He had been thinking the matter over, and he felt they could net do better in the matter of a perm ineut memor- ial than push forward the Cottage Holeital scheme to completion. (Applause.) He thought that scheme ought to have been carried into effect long ago. They had alreaey raised a nice sum towards the object, and they proposed to have the foundation stone laid on the 26th or 27th June, or on scene day near those dates which would meet with the wishes of all parties. They had a fired of £1,300 towards the schame. and they wanted to augment it to £2,000. (Applause.) He felt sure that the good work which would be accomplished by such an inatitutien would commend itself to all, and that every- ens in Runcorn would feel preud of having done seine thing toward the raising of that £2,000. With such a fund at their disposal they would be abla to equip and set the hospital going. Mr Marshall, Mr Wilding, and himself had drawn up resolutions for the covideration of the meeting and perhaps it would be well to place them before them at that stage. Mr Marshall tnen read the draft proposals, which were as f Mows :—... That the Coronation steal be cele- brated in Runcorn by (1) the giving of a tea to all the Sunday and day school children • (2), a treat to the aged persons ; (3), a procession Of magistrates, public authorities, clergymen, ministers, trade and friendly societies, &o• ; (4) a procession of Sunday schools ; (5), the holding of sports, bonfire, Sze. ; (6) by raising a fund for the establishmot of a cottage hospital as a perma- nent memorial of the Coronation ; and (7) by other means devised by the General Committee when ap pointed. - The Chairman said he would give £lOO to the Cottage Hospital scheme in addition to the £lOO he had already promised, and he would also give £2O towards the cemonstration fund. (Applause.) He would further present every boy and girl attending day or Sunday school, and each teacher belonging ta the day and Sun- day sohools with a medal. (Applause.) They thought the res lution3 read by Mr Marshall would meet with their approval, and he (the chairman) would either move them en bloc or separately. He had received a letter from Mr El Conereve regretting his inability to attend that meeting. Mr Congreve was very strongly in favour of this cottage hospital scheme. He had taken a deep interest in it from the start, although ho did not live in Runcorn,and he had promised £lOO towards the schema. (Applause.) Mr Imison asked if it was proposed that the celebra- tion should cover two days, or was the programme , drawn up to be carried out in one day. Were the sports I to he held separately from the demonstration, and would the procession be so arranged as it would not be likely to clash with any services that might be held ? The Chairmen suggested that the schools might have their proceasion in the afternoon of the first day. Mr Marshall, at this point, read a further resoletion to the effect that a general committee should be appointed to carry out the arrangements, consisting of the magis- trates of the Runcorn Petty Sessional Divisien,the mem- bers of the Urban District Council, the county coun- cillors representing Runcorn, the members of the School Board, the clergy and ministers, two representatives Ifrom each trade society, ta o from each Sunday school, two from each works, two from the Runcorn Co-opera- tive Society, two from the RuncorreCycle Club, and two I from the Runcorn Football Club, with power to add to , I its number. I

Mr Gatley said so farm he was concerned he would be quite willing,' to work with tbs friendly societies, but he suggested that to avoid any clashing the trades and frienoly societies should hold a huge demonstration on their own account.

The Chairman pointed out that these were matters of detail which might be left to the committee. Mr Aston moved that the programme as read out by Mr Marshall be adopted as far as possible, and that the suggested committee be appointed. Mr Posnett seconded. The first thing he would like to do WAS to congratulate the Ckairman upon the posi- tion be was holding in connection with this matter, and upon his occupancy of the chair of the District Council during the present year. (Applause). He was sure that in connection with these Coronation festivities ho would have the hearty support and good wishes of everybody in the town. That wao the essential thing they desired. They wanted to pull together, and to slar:w what their town could do in the matter of displaying its ;Igyalty. (Applause). Mr Handley pointed out that they had two days to fill up, and therefore they had more time in which to hold their festivities than they bad in 1897. It had occurred to him that they might very properly put the adults' portion of the festivities on the first day, and the juvenile portion on the second day. He suggested that on the first day they might have a procession of the friendly socioties,and also a procession of the representa- tive trades of the town. The latter, if properly organ- ized, would form a striking feature. The processions might be followed by good old English sports, which very few in Runcorn had seen. He remembered dimly the last old English sports which took place in Runcorn —that was in 1844 HO suggested that they might wisd up the day with a bonfire at night. Mr Aston, the mover of the resolution, thought that the church bells hould be rung and said he would like that added to his proposition. . . _

Canon Wood said that the people to decide whether the bells should be rung were the ringers themselves. They were rather too apt to get them to do their work and then fcrget about it afterwards. It should not be forgotten that at the end of the two days they would have been working all the time and have lost a good deal of the substance of their bodies. Still he had no doubt they would be only too pleased to ring the bells. Mr Taylor : Ido not think they will be forgottea, I will try to bear it in mind. (Applause.) Mr unison, moved in order to prevent any clashing with church services that the words be added to the resolution "that all the bands are arranged for the after- noon."

Mr Holt pointed out that most of the hand,' were already engaged for afternoon playing, and the town would be very lucky if they could secure their services other than for the morning. Mr F J Norman tbour;ht they were drifting into a lot of unnecessary details. The committee would fix the time of the procession at the most convenient time for everybody. As no sone seconded Mr Imison's rider, the original proposition was passed. On the proposition of the Chairman, Messrs Marahall and Wilding were appointed secretaries ; Messrs Shaw and Grice were appointed treasurers. Mr Handley pointed out besides voluntary subscrip- tions money would be required, and be thought they could not do better than allocate say • perma rate for the approaching festivities. It was hardly fair that a railway company who maie so much out of a town should not give their quota towards the fund. They would not voluntarily subscribe, and it was quite justi- fiable that they should pay through the rates. Mr F J Norman proposed that the meeting ask the Runcorn Urban Council to devote the sum of £2OO out of the rates to wards the Coronation festivities. It would be but a mere trifle from the working man and he hoped that the meeting would be perfectly unani- mous about it. Mr John Holt seconded .. _ •

--- The Chairman said he would not oppose the motion but he did not care for it. He would much rather they had got the money a ithout adopting such a measure, Tim motion was passed with only two dissentients. This concluded the meeting. Earlestown and Newton.

A meeting of the Coronation Committee was held in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening. Mr W Collingwood presided, and there was a good attend- ance of repres.ntatives from the Trades and other Socie- ties, school officials, ministers, and Sunday school rep- resentatives. A letter WAS read from Mr L.slie, agent to Lord Newton, grantidg the use of the Mesnes for the forrnation of a prceession. It was annltinced that the Earlesrown brass band and the Salvation Army band would give their services, but the Reformatory School band, owing to a prior engagement, could not attend, It was decided to invite Sunday school Bcholar3 to join

the procession, and to extend the invitation to the boys of the Reformatory School. It was also decided to ask the Trades and Friendly Societies to appoint represen- tatives to meet the sub-committee of the Council on Wednesday next at 7.30 p'm.—Votes of thanks to the Chairman closed the meeting.
THE EXAMINER FRIDAY MAY 2, 1902.

div.head: Penketh.
div.p: Penketh.

A meeting was held in the Wesleyan Schools, for the purpose of arranging for the coronation festivities. Dr Murray presided, arid there were also present :—llessrs J G Withinshaw, Coarlei E Parker, E W Clarke, J S Snoddy, J Millington, J B Aitken, J Dodds, P Grange, and E Foster (clerk to the Parish Council)._

Thal Chairman stated that the Parish Council were empowered to levy a rate to tie extent of 3.1 in the £ on the rates, to cover the cost of the festivities, and it this was not sufficient, tOey could (with the consent of a parish meeting) levy a rate to the extent of 6d in the £ but he did not think that would be necessary. . _

Mr Dodds said he thought there were not many amongst them who had taken part In a Coronation cele- bration. Ile proposed that the; do not levy a rate but provide the amount by private subscriptions, which wa3 agreed to. • It was also decided to entertain all the school children and aged people, over 60 years of age (residing in the township) to a substantial tea. Mr F W Gilbert and Mr Benjamin 1-1,31050 n were asked to become members of the committee.

div.head: Padgate.
div.p: Padgate.

At a meeting of the Coronation Committee, it was decided to divide the township into districts for the purpose of soliciting subscriptions and to request the f ollowing ladies to undertake the work, viz. :—Nlrs W Harris Wright and Miss Jackson (Manchester-road and Paddington), Miss Helen Bennett and Miss C J Bennett Green-lane, Padgate-lane and the Avenue), Miss Ada Birtles (Church-road and Fearnlaead-lane), and Miss May Gandy and Miss Birtles (Fearnhead Cross to Cinnamon Brow.) It was resolved to appoint sub-committees to arrange the sports, tea and procession, and the Secre- tary was instructed to ascertain the price of a band to play in the procession and f.old. Tao Committee invite and hope that the inhabitants will decorate and illumi- nate their houses on the 28th of June—the day of the festival.

div.head: Daresbury.
div.p: Daresbury.

A largely attended meeting was held in Daresbury Sessions Room, for the purpose of considering:details for carrying out:the proposedXoronation festival. The Vicar presided. and expressed his regret that the whole of the parish could not see their way to attend a central gathering at Daresbury. A letter was read from the clerk to the Moore Parish Council stating that at a meet- ing of ratepayer.; held in the township it had been decided to hold a fete of their own. A. deputution from Preston Brook attended the meeting and announced the decision of a portion of the township to hold their own gathering. The following were elected officers for the festivities at Daresbury :—President, :he Rev F Clifton Smith ; secretary, Mr John Wright ; treasurer, Mr C M Phillips. A general committee was appointed from the principal residents in Daresbury, liatton Keckwick, Newton-by-Daresbury, Mopre and Preston Brook, and arraripements made for a future meeting. It was also decided that the fete be held, if possible in the Elms Park.

div.head: Lymm. Proposed RecreationlGrounds.
div.p: Lymm. Proposed RecreationlGrounds.

A meeting was held in the Parochial Schools, Lymao, on Monday evening to hear the report of the committee appointed at a previous meeting, with reference to tho proposed purchase of land as a recreation ground, to form a permanent memorial of :the Coronation. Mr Groves, chairman of the Urban Council. presided. In making his report, the Rev G B Tourston 'said he had seen Mr Fairclough in reference to a plot of land which was very suitable for the purpose of a recreation ground. They would notice from a resolution:passed at a previous committee meeting that for the present, two playgroandsirnight be'provided—one in the Lymm parish and one in the Oughtrington parish. In company with others ho had had several interviews with Mr Fair- dough, with a view to obtaining the land at Newfields, but he was sorry to say that gentleman's decision was neither satisfactory nor encouraging. Mr Smith, in reperting re rbe Ooghtrington district said he had received a further reply stating that an offer of about £4OO, would be considered. If the idea of recreation grounds was to go on that was a very tempt- ing and reasonable offer, but as an alternative there was a plot of one acre in Sandy-lane. A long discussion took place, and it was decided that an att-mpt be made to actieire two plots of land, one in Newfislds and the other in Sandy-lane by purchase for the purposes of recreation grounds,and that a committee be appointed to further consider the matter and to arrange other details as t o the celebrations, &c. A committee having been appointed, the meeting concluded.

div.head: WARRINGTON SCHOOL HOLIDAYS:
div.p: WARRINGTON SCHOOL HOLIDAYS:
Meeting of Managers.

On Wednes lay evening a meeting, of Warrington school managers, convened by Allerman J Shaw Green (chairman of the School Attendance Committee,) was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall for the purpose of discussing the question of the date of the summer hoildays. Alderman Shaw Green presided over a good attendance. At the outset the Town. CLERK (Mr J Lyon Whittle) ' read the following letter addressed to Alderman Shaw Green by the Rev Morley Stevenson on March 24th : ** At a meeting of the cmamittee tie the Pupil Teachers Central Classes held on the 20th inst. (the Rev John I Yong° in the chair) the question of the date of the sum- mer holidays was considered. From the discussion that ensued it became evident that there was considerable diversity of opinion among the managers of schools aseto the most suitab:e date. It was felt trial the date of the holidays for the pupil teachers' centre must obviously be the same as that ot the schools and that if the date of the school holidays was not the same throughout the borough some pupil teachers would lose the whole or a part of their holidays. I was therefore instructed to ask you as chairman of the School Attendance Committee to consider the advisability of:summoniog a meeting of the managers of all the schools in the borough to endeavour to arrive at some agreement upon this matter." The Cam/amaze said the committee considered it a very important duty to endeavour to bring about a uni- form holiday. They had a meeting in that room some years ago and a very decided effort was made to arrange for the closiog, of the schools on one date in the year for the summer holidays. Unfortunately that fell through and they did cot feel for Some time afterwards that they could again attempt to bring about a sett ment of the question. The letter from Mr Stevenson brought forward the important question of endeavouring to arrange a general holiday to fit in with the pupil teachera' centre and it seemed to the committee to offer a suitable opportunity ef con- sidering the whole matter. He regretted, however, to find that between the date of Mr Stevenson's letter and the date of convening this meeting some meetings of school managers had been held. He had received the following letter, dated April G2tid, from the Rector (the Rev Canon Widis)--.. I have received your letter with notice of meeting on the 30th for which lain much ob- liged. lam sorry I did not know a little sooner of your intention. I have so cat's tried to obtain one and the Same time for all. but in vain, that I gave UP the attempt; so we had a meeting of our managers and head teachers the other day and following the precedent of last year which seemed to give general satisfaction, we unani- mously agreed to take the last week in July and the first three weeks in August which seemed to have so much to recommend it. We therefore, according to the present arrangerneate,hreak tin on Friday July 25'.11 and re-open on Monday, August 25th. This period covers the August Bank Holiday and breaks in the best place the long spell between Easter and Christmas. We tried three different times, two weeks in July and two in August, and four in August and we came to the conclusion that one in July and three in August was best . I shall

- hope the day we have chosen will recommend itself to you. There is much to recommend it, though, of course tbera is something to be said for an earlier date." Alderman Shaw Greee also reed a letter from Mr C Sawkins Burgess, stating that the holiday for St James's schools bad been fixed for the last week in July and the first three week 3 in August. The Chairman ex- pressed the hope that i':, would not be too late to alter these decisions if it were generaily ccnsidered that any date was more suitable. -

Tne Rceroa said a tiniform holiday would be a great advantage, and, speaking for himself, he would sink his own wishes in the matter if any time was generally agreed upon. The Rev J DAVIE 9 moved that the holidays shoulJ include Coronation week and three week zi afterwards, and that in future years tney should include Walking Day and the three weeks afterwards. .

The CHAIRMAN pointed out that they need not trouble about the future, as, if the Education Bill became law the local authority woJkl determine the question: This year it would have to be done by agrneMant. Councillor BAIRD seconded. . .

Alderman Masks aapported, and mentiened that tha managera of People College were in favour of that term and Mr Wallington bad also ascertained that the teaehers were favourable to it. lie did not think the managers would alter the date. - _

The proposition was supported by Councillor A J JOLLEY and the Rev John YONGE. 'Pao Rev Morley STEVENSON spoke in favour of a later date. He pointed out that people in their part of the town took a holiday diving tee are of Angu4t Bank Holiday and if the enhoolg were opened they would be altnost empty. Then again, there wal no examination in September and he thought that a month or six weeks was ample time for a school to get itself in romper trim and make a good show towards the end cf the school year. Would it not be possible to arrive at Some com- promise in order to secure that unanimity which they all desired ? In Liverpool it was possible to arrange a simultaneous holiday for every school and he thought it
would not be beyond the power of Warrington to do the same.
The CHAIRTifiN pointed out that Liverpool differed from Warrington, because Warrington had a local holi- day which Liverpool did not possess, between Whit week and August Bank Holiday. . . .

The Rev FATHER WILSON suggested that the holidays should commence on Jul; 11th acid end on August 11th. It seemed to him that that would meet a great many difficulties. and would at any rate be a compromise between the two extreme parties. Toe REcroa expressed his willingness to fall in with this arrangement but, of course, he could not speak for the other managers and teachers. In answer to the Rev John Tonga the CHAIRMAN said that if a resolution were passed it would not be binding upon the schools. It would simply be forwarded to the managers as the resolution of the meeting. Considerable discussion took place, Father Wilson remarking that he had a very vivid recollection that such a resolution was agreed upon by a large majority some years ago, and they bad not left the premises before it was quite evident that a good number of those present were not going to carry out the rosolution. It seemed to him that that was going to take place this year. . _

The Rev. JOHN YONGE said there was a statement abroad that the Mhz would desire the Cmonation week t-) ba kept as a noliday at tile echooll, and they as loyal people would not like to have their 'schools opeo if that wera 80.

The CHAIRMAN said the Town Clerk had no knowledge whatever of that suggestion. A resolution was adopted on the proposition of FATHER WILSON seconded by the HECTOR, " that it is desira.b,e that there should be a uniform holiday." The Rev J DAVIES then moved his resolation as to the date, welch was seconded by Alderman Malmo. The RECTR proposed that a strong effort be made to induce managers to arrange for the holidays to take place from July 11th to August 11th. Father WILSON seconded, and on a show of hands being taken, the Rector's proposition was carried by ten votes to seven. It was then derided to make the reso- lution unanimous by all agreeing to the proposition. The CHMRIVIAN pointed out that the schools which remained open during the time agreed upon for the holidays, would not receive tee same attention from th School Attend ince Committee as they otherwise would', : Tee TOWN,CLERK. wa iiisqm,,ted to send circulars to. all the ectio,3l :managers informing them of the decision of the meeting. The Rev MORLEY STEVENSON Said he wished to get some practical force if possible out of the meeting, and he moved a regolutba chat eaoh ga itleman present should undertake to use hi; utmost id' ience to obtain the carrying out of the decision of the meeting. The Rev Jolla; TONGS seconded and the proposition was agreed to. Thn meeting then terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above Council was held on Thursday at the Council Chamber. Present: Messrs 9 Taylor, J P (chairman), D Bisbrown, F Wiswall, M J Sweetman, W Handley, J HSalkeld, T Jones, E Gatley. J Wilson, J W Lightburn, I Pritchard, S Walton, J J Shaw, E Lrnison, G Hewitt, T Dean. E Marshall (secre- tary), F A Lake (law clerk), and J Wilding (surveyor). _

_ THE PARK. The Highways and Buildings Committee recommended ft at communications be addressed to the Sunday Schools intimating that the Common cannot be used dating the Whitsuntide holidays this year. Mr Handley in proposing the recommendation said that the Corr mon had recently been sown with 53 bustiEls of grass seeds at a cost of £45. If the schools were allowed to trample on the plots it would be so much money thrown away as it would spit the young grass. Mr Walton seconded and the minute was passed. EXAMINATION FEES.

The Technical Instruction Com-ra-ittee recommended that the Oxford Local Exarninati m fees be paid in res- pect of twenty-two holders of scholarsOips (twelve junior and senior and ten preliminary). Mr Wilsm, in proposing the adoption of the minute, saidlthat about 27 students were sitting for tie exami- nation and 22 were holders of scholarships. Mr Handley sec-mded and the minus were confirmed.

div.head: LATE ME. J. D. JONEEL
div.p: THE LATE ME. J. D. JONEEL

The Library Comm;t3ee recommended that Mr Handley be elected a metnber of the Committee, that the local books presented by Sir J T Brunner,be accepted and suitably acknowledged ; that the portrait of air J D Jones, the late librarian, subscribed for by the mem- bers of the Library Committee be presented to the Urban District Council of Runcorn, and that permission be asked to hang it on the Library wall. Mr Bisbrown proposed that the minutes be passed. The Committee, he said, desired that Sir Jolla Brunner be thanked for his generosity which they recognised. It woell be a pleasing thing to have the portrait of the late librarian on the wall, for he was a man who was everywhere remembered with respect. : The minutes were approved. ELECTIIIQ

A letter WA3 received from 51-6srs Rowcliffe and Co., Solicitors, Ceoss-street,Manchester, notifying their inten- tion to apply on behalf of a syndicate for parliamentary Powers to erect electric geoerating stations and lay mains for the supplying of electricity throughout a district comprising the county of Chester and the northern por- tion of the county of Stafford, and asking for the co- operation and help of the Council. Mr Wilson thought the matter should be referred to the taighways Committee which had to do with the light- ing up of the town and which was composed of the whole Council. Mr Wiswall seconded. Mr Handley suggested it should be referred to the Parliamentary C mumitttee. Mr L ike said that too Highway Committee was the proper committee to deal with it although it was Parliamentary work. After further discussion the. communication was re- ferred to the Highways Committee.

div.head: CORONATION FESTIVITIES.
div.p: THE CORONATION FESTIVITIES.
An order was read of the Local Government Board sanctinninv, any reasonable eapenses in connection with the public celebration of the Coroua'ion of His M3jesty the King.
The Chairman said that at a public mcetin7 held on lionday nis:ht, a resolutioo wa. n.ssed to ask tie Coun- cil to contribute Lys sum of £2OO out of the rates towards the demonstration.

Mr Marshall here read an account of the proceedings on Monday nigh: relating to the request for £2OO. Mr Handley as'red whether it was not necessary to suspend the standing orders ? Mr Lake said it would be, as there had not been any notice of motion on the subject. On the motion of Mr Handley the standing orders were suspended for the purpose of considering the request. Mr Irnisoo thou ht before the resolution was adopted some idea should be given as to what amount was rpent at the time of the jubilee celebration. Other rise they were in the dark whether the walnut was likely to he sufficient or more than sufficient. The effect on the financial position would be that instead of payieg off their liabilities—their income was £34 less than their expenditure and they expected to have an adverse balance of about £3o—that there would be a deficit of £230 instead of £3O. An extra rate would have to be put on to meet it though it would hardly be twopence. It would simply be £l4 more than tho product of a penny rate Mr Handley said that the proposal was received with such unanimity at the meeting on Monday that their Course was very clear. If they allocated £2OO nut of the rates it would only be in accordance with public opinion The majarity of tee towns about had allocated a sum equal to one penny in the £ Toe ranewel of footpaths for instance could easily be left for another year and none of the ratepayers would ohjact. Ile had pleasure In proposing that the sum or zor) tio allocated towards the coronation festivities out of the rates. The Chairman observed that if the town Was Pacing to do its share loyally it would tahe more like £4OO than £2OO. Runcorn would not be satisfied with being be- hind other towns.

Mr Flan lley reminded that he should have previously stated that Mr Taylor with his usual generosity had offered £2O towards the demonstration, bad offered to provide teachers and scholars with tnecials to celebrate the occasion and bad given £lOO to the cottage hospital to be erected as a permanent memorial of the coronation and the jubilee of the Cowl3il which occurred in mid- suramru, 1902.

Mr Prltcnard said he was preie.ct at Monday's melt- ing and 97aq atruck with the unanimity of feeling respecting the resolution. The burden on the rates could be spread over two years so that the working man wodld bear it very eas‘ily.

--Mrim-ison wondered whether Mr Bishrown was going, to give a silent vote on th 2 matter. They should be straightforward and honest in the matter. They always told the ratepayers they ha got to the very lowmt possible point in preparing the estimates and yet they were prop.-sing to spend mosey which had not been con- eidored• The exp6nditure was alre4dy not an irrAue- ible minimum. He did not think that the improvemente should be postponed. And he did not want anyone to think that th estimates had hem so loosely framed that they could afford to give £2OO out of them. . .

Mr Wiswall honed-he-wa -o-v-ai-su-b-js—cat, but he did net think they °null aff £2oo—eqcal to one penny on t'te rates. lie would like to know what towns were eivine, the rgeivalent to a nearly rate. If Liverplol or Manchester did so it wou'd mean a vast sum of money that wou'd surprise people. They could show their loyalty without spenclinq so him a sum of money. He was thinking of the poor people wile were struggling to pay their rates. He proposed that the amount be reduced by one half.

Mr Irnis-00, referring to the source from which the money had to come. said that if the money had had t 3 come Item the poor rate it would have been a mean thing to do. Coming out of the district rate made it fall:u pen property owners and large ratepayers. A man who tenanted a £6 house would not be called upon to pay anything at all. The Chairman asked it the Council did not vote the money where was it to come from ? There were many who could not voluntarily give who would be only too pleased to pay through their rates. The propoeition was carried, one or two abitaining from voting. THE EDUCATION BILL.

A circular was received from the Levensbuline Urban District Council enclosing copy of a resolution passed by such Council with regard to petitioning, the House of Comm ms praying for the amendment of Section 1 of the Education Bill by providing that Councils Of Urban Districts with a population of over 10,000 shall be the Local Education Authorities under the Act,and request- ing ths Runcorn Council to paSs a similar resolution.

Mr DA nn moved that the petitien b. senported. The bill in effect ssid that urban districts of 10,000 had uot as much sense as those ot 20,000. Re had as much com- monsee,e as a man who belonged to a borough and he resented the imputation reflscted on small councils. Mr Wiawall seconded.
Mr Imison proposed that it be reforrad to cormnittre. It wasimpossible at present to arrive at a proper decision °wine, to lack of details. .
_ After further discussion the communication was refer- red to the Geceral Purposes Committee.

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.

Cqptain E F Oakley, who has been on active ser- vice with the " Fighting 40h" (South Lance- shires) in South Africa,bas been selected for a home billet, and will take up the adjutancy of Colonel Pilkiugton's volunteer battalion of the South Lancashires. Captain Oakley has just completed 12 years' service. A Sr. HELENS ARTIST AT TIM ACADEMY.

Councillor Thomas EllisJr), one of the pr.oininent members of the St. Helens Sketching Club, has been honoured by having a water-colour accepted and hung at this year's exhibition at the Royal academy. This is, we believe, the first time such high honours have been woo by a St. Helens artist, and Mr Ellison has been most heartily coo gratulated by big °lntimates. The title of the accepted picture is "Cambrian Heights," the subject b lug a cloud-capped mountain, and a very clever a,mospheric effect has been obtained. The canvas is a good siz-ei one, and the sketch was made near Capel Cuing. Mr Ellison is one of the younger members of the St. Helens County Borough Council, and paints only in his spare time, being frilly occupiel in assisting in the management of his father's business of a contractor and builder.

div.head: WARRINGTON RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB. Review of -Season 1901-2.
div.p: WARRINGTON RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB. Review of -Season 1901-2.

[By "Ovemesra] The time for patting up the shutters. balancing the books, and taking stock of the accomplishments in the season 1901-2 has arrived. Rougoly speaking the Warrington Club has much more to congratu- late itself upon than mourn over, for at least one trophy has been secured as tangible proof of the abilities of the senior fifteen. Last season Warrington just missed both the Northern Union and West Lancashire cups after figuring in the final for each. On the last occasion they had small chance of gaining the former —such "opportunities are not vouchsafed very often—but they made amends by securing the trophy which stands as a reward for winning the South-West Lancashire and Border Towns Competi- tion—to give the full title—in which their prede- cessors competed successfully so long ago as the season 1886-7. Since that day the Warrington club was never honoured by the possession of a cup until Tuesday eveniug last when Widnes were routed in the deciding gems and the West Lanca- shire Cao fell to Warrington, together with a set of most handsome gold medals. This performance alone lifts the season jest concluded far above the rat of mediocrity, and the Club as a whole is en- titled to congratulations on the success which has been so honourably fouget for and gained. But, independently of the gratifsing issue of the West Lancashire Cup Competition, this has been no ordinary season. The formation of the Northern League, comprising the pick of Lancashire and Yorkshire Rugby clubs, was an event fraught with great responsibility to the Warringtoa club, its managers and players. They were called upon to compete in a higher sphere or class of football than had ever previously been the case, and the struegle to make a good show and pay the way promised to be a severe one. And it has. To the credit of all concerned the Warrington club has acquitted itself right well and in the new ',segue more points have been scored tnan have ever previously been gained by the Club in any competition under the auspices of which they have played. This in itself points, to the fact that the club was capable of rising to the occasion—which many people doubted at the commencement of September. The Committee had at their corainancl a body of young and energetic players, almost all of whom were local lads, and many of them just approaching their best days. With practically no outside tisistance an excellent record has been com- pile], and better football played than for many years past. Right at the outset a severe blow was dealt the club by the deduction of 2 points for a breach of the professional laws, Those two points had not nee been gain-d but they were at the expense of Batley in the first • League match oE the season, a victory particularly gratifying in the light of the result when the two teams met in the final at Leeds four mouths before. That score was paid off handsomely, Warrington patting up 15 points to Batley 3 points. Still the loss of those two points was felt all throueh the league tournament. At the very end of the journey the possession of them would erase) raised Warringtoa from seventh place in the list to the fifth, This League championship, as all know, was won be Broughton Rangers, who scored 43 points out of 26 matches, and were a clear 12 points ahead of their n-iarest:rivals,Salford. Only five points divided the next half-dozen clubs so that it will be seen how well Warrington have held their oivu in the good company to which they were silecte. Immediately following the opening marce with Batley, Warring- ton went to Bradford and astounded everybody by defeating the Yorkshire champions on their own ground, while later they twice defected Oldham and Runcorn, the Lancashire and Cheshire champions, to that the Northern Union Cup-holders:and the champions of Cheshire and of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Senior Competitions all fell before the prowess of the Warrington men. The first defeat was at the hands of the ultimate winners of the competition, Broughton Rangers, who won luckily on their own ground by 6 points to 5 points, The week after saw another most gratifying performance Warriagton beating Runcorn after failing to do so for many years. This feat was repeated at Runcorn later in the year. Throughout the season War- rington 'played with fair consistency, and away from home gave a particularly goad actount of themselves. Out of the 14 matches won in the League games, six victories were gained on foreign soil, and four of them in Yorkshire. Generally, I think. the Warrington men playea their best foot- ball away from home, for two or three defeats were sustained at Wilderspool through nothing but had play—notably the Swinton and Halifax matches. In the Northern Union Cup Competition Warrington defeated Barrow at home in mend land then went down badly before Bradford, who played a much superior game. In the second half of the season tne team was badly handicapped by the suspension of. Burgess and the injury , to the skipper, D Isherwood, who has been an enforced spectator since the end of January. With these two capable exponents available, Warrington must have gained several additional victories, but the (mis)fortunes of war have to be borne. At present the Club possesses a smart set of players, ' some of whom have noticeably improved, Burgess, Dickenson, Allen and Ilockenhall to wit, while the other old hands have all maintained their form. Edmonds and Roberts are two useful recruits from Birkenhead. The pi incipal weakness of the team is at present found in the forward division, where about 50 per cent. of new blood is urgently required. The scrimmaeers have quite failed to uphold the club's reputation either for strength or cleverness, and a big improvement here is a task which the Committee must at once set about per- forming. In other respects the available resources should enable the Club to hold its head high tor some time to come.

Financially, the Club has been very successful not- withstanding the increased expenaiture on the ground, in wages and travelimc expanses, and the loss cau,ed by postponed matches. There is at present some hing like £2OO cash in band as well as money invested in the Cor- poration. The liabilities of the club it h at prsent impossible to compute, but there is no doubt that a pralt has been made on the year's working—a fact which will rouse envy in the breasts of most other Northern Leas tiers. The Works' Competition has again been held and has justified its existence by producing a revenue somewhat larger than that of last season, and also some very good games between the 24 clubs who entered. The final tie on Saturday was between Fletcher Russell's and Messrs Naylor's men, the former winning the medals for the second time since the inauguration of the competition. A good sum will again be available for charities. Coming once more to statistics, thirty-eight matches have been played by the first team during the season just closed, and of thee) twenty-three have been won, fouteeen lost, and one drawn. Warrington defeated twice, South Shields, Runcorn, Oldham, Brighouse Ran- gers, St. Helene, Huddersfield, Hull, and Wigan. They were beaten twice by Bradford, Broughton Rangers, Swinton, Halifax, and Salford, while single victories were gained at the expense of Batley, Bradford, Leigh, Hunslet, Widnes, Barrow, and Birkenhead Wanderers. The only draw of the sea-on was with Widnes at War- ringtou. on February 22. The particulars of every match in the past season are as follows : DATE. 19.11.

A meeting of the Great Sankey School Board was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Board room at the schools,the chair being taken by Mr Thomas Halton. There were also present : Messrs Perks, i ulton Smite, and J Wright, and Mr W D Jeans, jun. (clerk to the Board). The Clerk produced an estimated account for the half-year ending September, 1002, from which it appeared that the bank balance was £220 Os 21, less uncashed cheques £S7G; 6d. There was receivable from the Educt lon Department a fee grant of £64 10s; grant under the Agricultural Rating Act. £lB 78 41 ; school fees, £2O. The amount required from the overseers was £105. The Chairman remarked that in addition to the attempted burglarly at the schools, there had been attempts in various parts of the district, including his own house. lie considered that the police authorities had made a great mistake by placing the two police in one position.—Mr Fulton Smit'a They are both together now; before they ware too far apart—The Caairman : It is high time there was a police-office built in this district. The ser- geant and the police both live at Sankey Bridges. Ours is a populous district now, and when you recollect that the road outside is the main road between Liverpool and Man- chester, and that all sorts of individuals use it. I think you will admit it is high time something was done to protect our interests--Mr Fulton Smith : And burglars will get to know of the existing arrangement. I was surprised to hear that the officers had gone to the same place.—The Chairman: I understood it was because there was no suitable house for the constable.—Mr Wright : Well, the county authorities should build their own house.— The Chairman : We ought to have a police station in Sankey —lt was stated that the matter would be discussed at the Parish Council meeting. Railway Signalman, Blackbank, near Ely, Cambridge- shire, writes :—" I feel it my duty to explain to you the great benefit I have derived through drinking Vi-Cocoa, which I have done for the past three years. Previously, I used to drink tea, but was obliged to give it up, as I used to suffer from pains in the back and body; but since I have been drinking Vi-Cocoa, I am a different man and weigh two stone heavier than I did three years ago. "I am a Great Eastern Railway signalman, and have to do day and night duty three weeks about. When on night duty, I hot my can upon the stove, and have a cup when I feel thirsty; it is as fresh in the morning as it is when put in the can at night Tea used to make me feel faint, but now, thank God, my work in the box is not nearly so hard to me. "I have recommended Vi-Cocoa to my fellow-workmen, and they have commenced to use it.
